ch03.note: Kong Congzhou (1906-1991), a secret Communist within Yang Hucheng's forces who later became a general of the People's Liberation Army.

ch03.anchor: go and look up Mr. Du Binchen
ch03.note: Du Binchen (1888-1947), a Shaanxi educator and statesman close to Yang Hucheng and sympathetic to the Communists; he was executed by the Kuomintang in 1947.

ch03.anchor: August First Declaration
ch03.note: The 'August First Declaration' of August 1, 1935, issued from Moscow in the name of the Chinese Communist Party and the Chinese Soviet government, called on all parties and armies to stop the civil war and unite against Japan; it was an early public statement of the united-front line.

ch03.anchor: had sent Shen Bochun to see him there
ch03.note: Shen Bochun (1898-1979), a go-between in the early contacts with Yang Hucheng, later an official in the People's Republic.

ch03.anchor: one of his division commanders, Feng Qinzai
ch03.note: Feng Qinzai (1889-1963), a division commander under Yang Hucheng who broke with him and sided with Chiang at the time of the Xi'an Incident.

ch03.anchor: the Communist Yan Kuiyao
ch03.note: Yan Kuiyao (1904-1994), then a regimental commander in Yang Hucheng's forces and a secret Communist, later a lieutenant general and senior staff officer of the People's Liberation Army.

ch03.anchor: help Wu Xiru run the Cultural Weekly
ch03.note: Wu Xiru (1906-1985), a left-wing writer and Communist who edited the Cultural Weekly under the cover of Zhang Xueliang's Northeastern Army.

ch03.anchor: the left-wing writers Xu Pingyu and Ding Ling
ch03.note: Ding Ling (1904-1986), one of the best-known writers of the Chinese left, whose fiction of women's lives had made her famous before she reached the Communist areas; she would herself fall foul of the very campaigns this chapter describes. Xu Pingyu (1909-1986) was a left-wing writer and, in the People's Republic, a cultural official.

ch03.anchor: founded by the Anti-Japanese Comrades' Association
ch03.note: The Anti-Japanese Comrades' Association (Kang-Ri Tongzhi Hui), a secret patriotic body within Zhang Xueliang's Northeastern Army that pressed for resistance to Japan and cooperation with the Communists.

ch03.anchor: Red China News Agency
ch03.note: The Red China News Agency (Hongse Zhonghua Tongxunshe), the Communist Party's wire service in the Soviet areas and the direct forerunner of the New China (Xinhua) News Agency; its Xi'an branch relayed Party news and documents during the united-front period.

ch03.anchor: Li Yimang of the Shaanxi provincial committee
ch03.note: Li Yimang (1903-1990), a writer and Party official, later prominent in the People's Republic's cultural and foreign-liaison work.

ch03.anchor: the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region
ch03.note: The Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, the Communist base around Yan'an spanning parts of Shaanxi, Gansu, and Ningxia, and the Party's seat of government through the war years.

ch03.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek's loyal general Hu Zongnan
ch03.note: Hu Zongnan (1896-1962), the Whampoa-trained general Chiang trusted to hold the northwest and blockade the Communist base at Yan'an; his headquarters made Xi'an a nerve center of Nationalist intelligence.

ch03.anchor: with Wu Defeng in charge
ch03.note: Wu Defeng (1896-1976), head of the Party's Xi'an intelligence station, later a mayor of Wuhan and a judicial official in the People's Republic.

ch03.anchor: the Lugou Bridge Incident of July 1937
ch03.note: The Lugou Bridge, or Marco Polo Bridge, Incident of July 7, 1937, the clash outside Beijing that opened the full-scale war between China and Japan.

ch03.anchor: Chen worked with Nan Hanchen, Liu Ding, Xuan Xiafu, Xu Binru
ch03.note: Xuan Xiafu (1899-1938), a Communist active in united-front and military work, murdered by Kuomintang agents in 1938; Xu Binru (1901-1980), a Communist historian later prominent in the museums of the People's Republic.

ch03.anchor: such as Du Binchen, Li Furen, Gao Chongmin, Yang Mingxuan
ch03.note: Prominent Xi'an patriots of the resistance period: Li Furen (1895-1975), a journalist and educator; Gao Chongmin (1891-1971), a founder of the China Democratic League; Yang Mingxuan (1891-1967), an educator and later a vice-governor of Shaanxi; with them Han Zhuoru, Che Xiangchen, and Xu Zhongquan, figures of the local resistance and cultural world.

ch03.anchor: the Central Social Affairs Department at Yan'an
ch03.note: The Central Social Affairs Department (Zhongyang Shehui Bu), the Party's central intelligence and security organ, set up in 1939 under Kang Sheng; it directed both foreign intelligence and internal security and was an ancestor of the later state security services.

ch03.anchor: sponsored by Comrades Luo Qingchang and Qiu Jin
ch03.note: Luo Qingchang (1918-2014), a career intelligence officer who rose to head the Party's investigation department in later decades. The Qiu Jin here is a Yan'an cadre, not the revolutionary martyr of 1907 whose name has the same sound.

ch03.anchor: Elder Sister Deng Yingchao
ch03.note: Deng Yingchao (1904-1992), a women's leader and Zhou Enlai's wife, herself a veteran revolutionary; 'Elder Sister Deng' (Deng dajie) was the affectionate name comrades used for her.

ch03.anchor: just then Yan'an was launching the Rectification Movement
ch03.note: The Yan'an Rectification Movement (zhengfeng, 1942-1945), the Party's campaign to unify thought around Mao's line through study, criticism, and self-criticism. It consolidated Mao's leadership; but its later cadre-vetting phase, driven by Kang Sheng, turned into the persecutions this chapter goes on to describe.

ch03.anchor: study at the Central Party School
ch03.note: The Central Party School at Yan'an, the Party's senior training academy; Mao took over as its principal in 1943, making it a center of the Rectification.

ch03.anchor: Wu Xiru and Wang Shiwei
ch03.note: Wang Shiwei (1906-1947), a writer at Yan'an whose essay 'Wild Lilies' attacked privilege and inequality among the leadership; made a central target of the Rectification, branded a Trotskyite, and secretly executed in 1947. His case became a byword for the campaign's excesses, and he was posthumously cleared in 1991. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: It was in these three branches that Jiang Qing and Ye Qun were vetted
ch03.note: Jiang Qing (1914-1991), a former Shanghai actress who married Mao Zedong in Yan'an and, three decades later, led the ultra-left Gang of Four in the Cultural Revolution, to be tried and imprisoned after Mao's death. Ye Qun (1917-1971), who married the marshal Lin Biao, died with him in the 1971 plane crash after his failed move against Mao. That the young Chen Yangshan's branch reviewed the wartime histories of both women is among the striking details of this account.

ch03.anchor: the "Three People's Principles Youth Corps"
ch03.note: The Three People's Principles Youth Corps (Sanqingtuan), the Kuomintang's youth organization, founded in 1938; membership in it was treated in the Rectification as the mark of a suspect past.

ch03.anchor: the so-called "Movement to Rescue the Fallen" was launched
ch03.note: The 'Movement to Rescue the Fallen' (qiangjiu shizuzhe) of 1943, the coercive high point of the Rectification's cadre-vetting, in which Kang Sheng's methods extracted mass false confessions of spying; thousands were wrongly branded enemy agents before Mao ordered the campaign reined in. Later Party verdicts admit these excesses. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: The Party's Seventh Congress was also about to open
ch03.note: The Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party in fact met from April 23 to June 11, 1945, not 1943 as this and the following paragraphs have it. The error is the source's; Mao's own words below, on 'the twenty-four years of our Party's course,' count from the Party's founding in 1921 to 1945, and the membership figures given (1.2 million members, nearly a million troops) are those of 1945. The congress enshrined Mao Zedong Thought in the Party constitution and chose the leadership that would win the civil war.

ch03.anchor: with Mao Zedong himself as principal and Peng Zhen as deputy
ch03.note: Peng Zhen (1902-1997), a leading Party organizer, later mayor of Beijing and the first senior figure purged at the outset of the Cultural Revolution; rehabilitated, he helped rebuild the legal system in the 1980s.

ch03.anchor: Ren Bishi first reported on how the congress had been prepared
ch03.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950), one of the five secretaries of the Party's wartime leadership alongside Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, and Zhu De; he died young, in 1950.

ch03.anchor: The "Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of the Party,"
ch03.note: The 'Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of the Party,' adopted in 1945, was the Party's authoritative reckoning with its past line struggles; it fixed the verdict that Mao's leadership had rescued the revolution from a succession of erroneous lines.

ch03.anchor: Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, Lin Boqu, and Okano Susumu
ch03.note: Zhu De (1886-1976), commander-in-chief of the Red Army and later the People's Liberation Army; Liu Shaoqi (1898-1969), the Party's leading organizer and later head of state, who died in prison during the Cultural Revolution; Lin Boqu (1886-1960), a revolutionary elder. Okano Susumu was the alias used in Yan'an by Nosaka Sanzo (1892-1993), a founder of the Japanese Communist Party who spent the war years with the Chinese Communists organizing anti-war work among Japanese prisoners.

ch03.anchor: "On Coalition Government," and had a copy given to every delegate
ch03.note: 'On Coalition Government,' Mao Zedong's political report to the Seventh Congress in 1945, set out the Communist program for the end of the war and after: a coalition to replace one-party Kuomintang rule, and the building of a 'new-democratic' China.

ch03.anchor: again proposed five Marxist-Leninist works
ch03.note: The five works were the touchstones of orthodox Marxism-Leninism then: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto and Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific; Lenin's Two Tactics of Social-Democracy in the Democratic Revolution and 'Left-Wing' Communism, an Infantile Disorder; and the Stalin-era History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks), the 'Short Course.'

ch03.anchor: studying at Zaoyuan in Yan'an
ch03.note: Zaoyuan, 'the orchard,' a compound outside Yan'an that housed the Party's central leadership and the Social Affairs Department in the war years.

ch03.anchor: the "April Third Decision,"
ch03.note: The 'April Third Decision' properly names the Central Committee's decision of April 3, 1943 on carrying the Rectification forward; this recollection places it in the spring of 1942, when the Rectification was first launched.

ch03.anchor: the Investigation Bureau of the Jin-Sui Military Region
ch03.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Military Region, a Communist command in northwestern Shanxi and beyond under He Long; its investigation bureau handled intelligence and security.

ch03.anchor: Kirov, a member of the Politburo of the CPSU Central Committee
ch03.note: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad Party boss, was assassinated on December 1, 1934; Stalin used his murder as the pretext for the purges and show trials that became the Great Terror of 1936-1938. The 'third year' places this account in 1937, at the Terror's height.

ch03.anchor: The head of the CCP delegation to the Communist International was Wang Ming
ch03.note: The Communist International, or Comintern, was the Moscow-based body directing the world's Communist parties. Wang Ming (Chen Shaoyu, 1904-1974) led the 'returned students' faction and the CCP delegation to the Comintern; his rivalry with Mao runs through the Party's history of these years, and he spent his last decades in the Soviet Union attacking Mao.

ch03.anchor: suppress counter-revolutionaries and root out Trotskyites
ch03.note: The Soviet purge and its anti-Trotskyist drive swept up foreign Communists resident in the USSR along with Soviet citizens; a number of Chinese Communists studying or working in Moscow were arrested and shot in 1937-1938. That these deaths happened is well attested; how far Kang Sheng personally engineered particular cases, as the book charges, rests largely on testimony gathered in China after his fall.

ch03.anchor: Xiao Shouhuang, Ouyang Xin, and He Changzhi
ch03.note: Xiao Shouhuang, Ouyang Xin, and He Changzhi were Chinese Communist cadres, formerly of the Central Special Branch, sent to study in the Soviet Union in 1935 and killed there in the purge of 1937-1938. The Party rehabilitated them after 1978. The book gives their names as Chen Yangshan remembered them; some appear in other records under variant characters.

ch03.anchor: Wu Hujing was a Shandong man
ch03.note: Wu Hujing (1904-1938), also known as Wu Huairang, a senior Communist organizer who had led the Party's work in northern Manchuria and in the Central Special Branch; sent to Moscow in 1935, he was arrested and shot in the Soviet purge. His wife was the revolutionary Hou Zhi. He was posthumously rehabilitated.

ch03.anchor: Kang Sheng's own sister-in-law, Su Mei
ch03.note: Su Mei was a sister of Kang Sheng's wife, Cao Yi'ou; that she went to the Soviet Union with the others yet came to no harm is the circumstantial point Chen Yangshan presses against Kang.

ch03.anchor: Kang Sheng was head of its Action Section
ch03.note: The Action Section (xingdong ke) was the Special Branch's armed arm, the 'Red Squad' whose killings of traitors filled the previous chapter; Kang Sheng directed it in the early 1930s.

ch03.anchor: the anti-Party crimes of Lin Biao and the "Gang of Four"
ch03.note: Lin Biao (1907-1971), the marshal named as Mao's successor, who died in a plane crash over Mongolia in 1971 after an alleged plot against Mao. The Gang of Four (Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen) were the ultra-left leaders of the Cultural Revolution, arrested in 1976; the reckoning with their 'crimes' was the moment Chen Yangshan's charges against Kang Sheng were laid before the Party.

ch03.anchor: there must be no "coercion, confession, and credence."
ch03.note: 'Coercion, confession, credence' (bi, gong, xin): the vicious circle in which torture ('coercion') produces false confessions, which are then 'believed' and used to force fresh arrests. Mao's warnings against it, quoted here, were aimed at the very campaign Kang Sheng was running.

ch03.anchor: in the days of the Central Soviet Area
ch03.note: The Central Soviet Area in Jiangxi (1931-1934), the Communists' main base before the Long March, where an earlier internal purge (the anti-'AB' campaign, and the Futian Incident of 1930) had killed many of the Party's own; that was the bitter lesson Mao invokes.

ch03.anchor: in 1980 the Party Center decided to expel him from the Party
ch03.note: Kang Sheng (1898-1975) died honored; only in 1980, as the Party reckoned with the Cultural Revolution, was he posthumously expelled and his ashes removed from the Babaoshan cemetery of revolutionary martyrs. It is this official verdict that lets the book state his guilt so flatly.

ch03.anchor: To the Central Organization Department, and to the Ministry of State Security
ch03.note: The Ministry of State Security, the People's Republic's civilian intelligence and security ministry, was formed in 1983; its inclusion as an addressee fits the letter's 1988 date.

ch03.anchor: Xiao Shouhuang (from Dapu, Guangdong)
ch03.note: Dapu is the county of Dabu in eastern Guangdong (the source writes the place-name with a homophone). 'Lao Da,' 'Lao Wang,' and 'Lao Hu' that follow are the men's familiar nicknames, not surnames.

ch03.anchor: Chiang went to Xi'an to direct the fighting
ch03.note: Xi'an (西安), the great city of the northwest and capital of Shaanxi province, was one of imperial China's ancient capitals. In the mid-1930s it was the seat of Yang Hucheng's Seventeenth Route Army and the forward base from which Chiang Kai-shek directed the campaign against the Communists in northern Shaanxi.

ch03.anchor: In several battles in northern Shaanxi
ch03.note: Northern Shaanxi (Shaanbei, 陕北), the arid loess-hill country in the north of the province, was where the Red Army ended the Long March in 1935 and built the base area that became the Communist heartland, centered first on Wayaobao and Bao'an and from 1937 on Yan'an.

ch03.anchor: sat on the mountain to watch the tigers fight
ch03.note: A common set phrase, zuo shan guan hu dou (坐山观虎斗): to sit on the mountain and watch two tigers fight, letting rivals wear each other down before stepping in. The charge here is that Chiang Kai-shek meant the Red Army and the Northeastern Army to destroy one another.

ch03.anchor: near Wayaobao
ch03.note: Wayaobao (瓦窑堡), a walled town in Zichang county in northern Shaanxi that served as the Communists' provisional capital in 1935–36. It gave its name to the Party conference of December 1935 that adopted the line of an anti-Japanese national united front.

ch03.anchor: Li Kenong reached Luochuan
ch03.note: Luochuan (洛川), a county on the road south from the Communist base toward Xi'an, then inside the lines of Zhang Xueliang's Northeastern Army. It would later host the Party's Luochuan Conference of August 1937, which set Communist strategy for the war against Japan.

ch03.anchor: Fushi (now Yan'an)
ch03.note: Fushi was the old name of Yan'an (延安), the town in northern Shaanxi that from the end of 1936 became the seat of the Chinese Communist Party and the capital of its wartime base area. Through 1947 the name 'Yan'an' stood for the Party's leadership and its whole revolutionary center.

ch03.anchor: trade between Red and White areas
ch03.note: In the color-coding of the civil-war years, 'Red' areas were those the Communists governed and 'White' areas those held by the Kuomintang; the 'white terror' mentioned later is the Nationalist suppression carried on in the latter.

ch03.anchor: crossed east over the Yellow River
ch03.note: The Red Army's Eastern Expedition (dongzheng, 东征): from February 1936 the main Red Army crossed the Yellow River eastward into Shanxi, fought the warlord Yan Xishan's forces for some seventy-five days while recruiting men and raising funds, and withdrew back into Shaanxi in May. Shilou, named here, was one of the Shanxi counties it passed through.

ch03.anchor: force Chiang to resist Japan
ch03.note: Bi Jiang kang Ri (逼蒋抗日). In the course of 1936 the Communists shifted their slogan from 'oppose Chiang and resist Japan' to 'force Chiang to resist Japan'—pressing Chiang Kai-shek to turn his armies against the invader rather than seeking to overthrow him—a change that prepared the way for the second united front.

ch03.anchor: Nan had been Yang's chief secretary
ch03.note: Nan Hanchen (南汉宸, 1895–1967), a Shanxi Communist long tied to Yang Hucheng's circle, who directed the Party's covert liaison and finance work in north China. After 1949 he became the first governor of the People's Bank of China. He died a victim of the Cultural Revolution.

ch03.anchor: great northwestern alliance
ch03.note: The plan, canvassed in 1936, for a 'great northwestern alliance'—a Northwest National Defense Government joining the Red Army with Zhang Xueliang's Northeastern Army and Yang Hucheng's Northwestern Army in a resistance bloc across the northwest. It was set aside late in 1936 as Communist policy turned toward a nationwide united front that would include Chiang.

ch03.anchor: director of the Xi'an Pacification Office
ch03.note: The Xi'an Pacification (or Bandit-Suppression) Headquarters (西安绥靖公署), the military-administrative command through which Yang Hucheng governed Shaanxi under the Nationalist government.

ch03.anchor: the Party Center's Xi'an intelligence station
ch03.note: The Party Center's clandestine intelligence station in Xi'an, run under the Military Commission's liaison system. Set up in the spring of 1936, it gathered military and political intelligence and worked united-front contacts in the city; its operations are the subject of much of this chapter.

ch03.anchor: director of the Northwest Culture Daily in Xi'an
ch03.note: The Northwest Culture Daily (西北文化日报), a Xi'an newspaper close to Yang Hucheng's Seventeenth Route Army; during the Xi'an Incident it printed the two generals' manifesto. Its director, Song Qiyun, was a secret Communist, which is how Chen Yangshan obtained his cover as a reporter there.

ch03.anchor: the Eighth Route Army's Xi'an office at Qixianzhuang
ch03.note: The Eighth Route Army (八路军) was the Red Army reorganized in 1937 under nominal Nationalist command for the war against Japan. Its Xi'an liaison office, at Qixianzhuang ('the manor of the seven worthies') on the city's north side, was the Communists' open agency there, forwarding recruits and supplies to Yan'an; it operated until 1946.

ch03.anchor: the study movement to rectify the three work-styles
ch03.note: The 'three work-styles' (san feng, 三风) were the three targets of the Rectification: subjectivism in study and thought, sectarianism in Party conduct, and stereotyped, formulaic writing (党八股). The campaign set out to remold each through study and self-criticism.

ch03.anchor: and the vetting of cadres began
ch03.note: The vetting or screening of cadres (shen'gan, 审干): the organizational phase of the Rectification, in which each cadre's personal and political history was investigated for hidden enemies. Pushed to extremes in 1943, it produced the coercive 'Rescue' campaign described below.

ch03.anchor: Song Shilun, Wang Heshou, Xiang Zhonghua
ch03.note: Song Shilun (宋时轮, 1907–1991), a Hunanese and Whampoa graduate, later one of the People's Liberation Army's senior commanders; in the Korean War he led the Ninth Army Group against the Americans at the Chosin Reservoir. The others named here were fellow students at the Party School, among them Wang Heshou (王鹤寿), later minister of metallurgy.

ch03.anchor: Mo Wenhua, Zeng Zhi, and Kang Keqing
ch03.note: Mo Wenhua (莫文骅, 1910–2000), a political officer later made a lieutenant general of the People's Liberation Army; Zeng Zhi (曾志, 1911–1998), a veteran woman revolutionary and wife of Tao Zhu; and Kang Keqing (康克清, 1911–1992), a Long March veteran and the wife of Zhu De. All three led branches at the Central Party School during the cadre vetting.

ch03.anchor: Question of the Two Lines
ch03.note: The 'question of the two lines' (两条路线) was the Party's account of its own past as a struggle between a 'correct' line, identified with Mao, and a series of 'erroneous' lines. Senior cadres studied it to arrive at the verdict later fixed in the 1945 Resolution on Party history.

ch03.anchor: Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu
ch03.note: Communist base areas were named by one-character abbreviations of the provinces they spanned: Jin (晋) is Shanxi, Ji (冀) Hebei, Lu (鲁) Shandong, Yu (豫) Henan. Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu was thus the Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan border base on the north China plain.

ch03.anchor: and the Great Rear Area
ch03.note: The 'Great Rear Area' (da houfang, 大后方) was the unoccupied southwest and northwest still under Nationalist rule during the war, the country behind the front, where the Communists maintained an underground. Its congress delegates had to travel in secret out of Kuomintang territory.

ch03.anchor: the Central Intelligence Department sent Chen Yangshan
ch03.note: The Central Intelligence Department (中央情报部), the Party's central intelligence organ established at Yan'an in 1941 and run jointly with the Central Social Affairs Department under Kang Sheng, and later Li Kenong. The two shared staff and were in effect one body under two names.

ch03.anchor: Nine-Point Policy
ch03.note: The 'Nine-Point Policy' (九条方针) was the set of nine principles Mao laid down for cadre vetting—leadership taking responsibility, evidence over confession, winning back the fallen, and the rest—set squarely against the 'coercion, confession, credence' of the Rescue campaign.

ch03.anchor: Yuan Renyuan, the commissioner for Suide
ch03.note: Yuan Renyuan (袁任远), a veteran Communist administrator, then the Party's commissioner (专员) for the Suide district on the northern edge of the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region.

ch03.anchor: the Central General Study Committee
ch03.note: The Central General Study Committee (中央总学习委员会) was the top body directing the Rectification study campaign across the whole Party; it was chaired by Mao Zedong with Kang Sheng as his deputy.

ch03.anchor: Great Cultural Revolution
ch03.note: The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (无产阶级文化大革命, 1966–1976), the upheaval Mao launched to purge his rivals and rekindle the revolution, in which Kang Sheng and the 'Gang of Four' hounded and persecuted vast numbers of officials. It is treated at greater length later in the book.

ch03.anchor: mild as a gentle rain
ch03.note: An idiom, hefeng xiyu (和风细雨), literally 'gentle breeze and fine rain,' for methods that are mild and persuasive rather than harsh—the opposite of the coercive struggle that soon followed.

ch04.anchor: The Jin-Sui Border Region was one of the principal revolutionary base areas
ch04.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Border Region was a Communist base area straddling northwestern Shanxi and the neighboring province of Suiyuan (now largely central Inner Mongolia), established during the war against Japan and led from Xingxian. Its value, as the text says, lay in its position screening the Party's Yan'an headquarters in the Shaan-Gan-Ning region and linking it to the areas beyond; the claim that it was the “one artery” to Outer Mongolia and the Soviet Union is the book's own emphasis, corroborated in broad outline by histories of the base area, which stress its role as a corridor and shield rather than a major fighting front.

ch04.anchor: Luo Qingchang has recalled
ch04.note: Luo Qingchang (1918–2004) was a career Communist intelligence officer who rose to head the Central Investigation Department (the CCP's foreign-intelligence organ) and was long one of Zhou Enlai's trusted men on the hidden front; he is remembered for the deathbed charge Zhou gave him in 1975 concerning Taiwan. At its first appearance here (printed p. 106) the source prints his name with the characters transposed, as “Luo Changqing” (罗长青); it gives the correct form “Luo Qingchang” (罗青长) five pages on. Both are rendered here by the correct name.

ch04.anchor: had Stalingrad fallen, the world revolution would have entered a dark time
ch04.note: The Battle of Stalingrad (August 1942 to February 1943) was the turning point of the Soviet-German war; a German victory there was widely feared at the time to open the way to a Japanese-German linkup across Eurasia. Luo Qingchang's remark reflects the anxiety in Yan'an that the fall of the Soviet Union would have isolated the Chinese revolution.

ch04.anchor: we built a base in the Daqing Mountains
ch04.note: The Daqingshan (Great Blue Mountains) guerrilla base was a Communist foothold in the mountains north of Guisui (Hohhot) in Suiyuan, opened in 1938 by a detachment under Li Jingquan and Yao Zhe; it extended the Jin-Sui area's reach toward Mongolia and the Sino-Soviet frontier.

ch04.anchor: push the "Gao Shuxun Movement" forward vigorously
ch04.note: The “Gao Shuxun Movement” was a Communist campaign, named for the Nationalist general Gao Shuxun, to induce Nationalist officers to defect rather than fight in the civil war. Gao (1898–1972), a deputy commander in the Eleventh War Zone, crossed over with his troops at the Handan front on October 30, 1945; Mao Zedong seized on the example and called in early 1946 for the systematic organizing of such revolts. The campaign is treated at length later in this chapter.

ch04.anchor: He Long and Li Jingquan spoke at a public-security conference
ch04.note: Li Jingquan (1909–1989) was a senior political commissar of the Jin-Sui base area and its military region, later first Party secretary of Sichuan and a Politburo member; he was purged in the Cultural Revolution and rehabilitated afterward. He Long, the region's commander and Chen Yangshan's old protector, is introduced earlier in the book.

ch04.anchor: a section of the Bureau of Confidential Investigation's organization in southern Shanxi
ch04.note: The Bureau of Confidential Investigation (Baomiju, 保密局) was the Nationalist secret service formed in 1946 from the wartime Juntong (Bureau of Investigation and Statistics); it ran counter-Communist agent networks until 1949. It recurs through this chapter as the chief adversary of Chen Yangshan's stations.

ch04.anchor: and by Chiang (Kai-shek), Yan (Xishan), and Fu (Zuoyi)
ch04.note: Yan Xishan (1883–1960) was the warlord who governed Shanxi from 1911 until 1949, notorious for keeping thousands of surrendered Japanese troops in his service after 1945 (mentioned below); he fled to Taiwan and briefly served as the Republic of China's premier. Fu Zuoyi (1895–1974) was the Nationalist commander in Suiyuan and later North China, who surrendered Beiping peacefully in January 1949 and went on to serve the People's Republic as minister of water resources. Chiang Kai-shek is noted earlier.

ch04.anchor: secret talks between the puppet forces and Yan Xishan's representatives
ch04.note: After Japan's surrender Yan Xishan raced to take over the puppet garrisons and Japanese arms in Shanxi before the Communists could, and secretly retained several thousand Japanese soldiers (see below) to hold Taiyuan. Communist intelligence tracking these contacts is the subject of much of this chapter.

ch04.anchor: Tan Zhengwen as director and Chen Yangshan as deputy director
ch04.note: Tan Zhengwen (1910–1961) was a leading Communist security official, head of the Jin-Sui public-security apparatus and later a deputy procurator-general of the People's Republic. His transfer in 1947 (noted below) left Chen Yangshan as director.

ch04.anchor: with Ma Mingfang, deputy secretary of the Northwest Bureau
ch04.note: Ma Mingfang (1905–1974) was a veteran Communist organizer of the Shaanxi base areas, later a deputy secretary of the CCP Northwest Bureau and a national labor and organization official; he was persecuted to death in the Cultural Revolution.

ch04.anchor: and it was through the Special Branch, through Comrade Chen Yangshan's arrangements, to be exact, that I was hidden in Shanghai and then secretly moved on to Honghu
ch04.note: Honghu (“Vast Lake”), on the Hubei-Hunan border, was the heart of the Xiang-E-Xi soviet that He Long and Zhou Yiqun built after the Nanchang Uprising of 1927. He Long's escape from Shanghai to Honghu, arranged by the Special Branch, is told in Chapter 1; his gratitude is why he asked for Chen Yangshan by name in 1944.

ch04.anchor: Pei Zhouyu, then deputy director of the Jin-Sui Border Region Public Security Bureau, has recalled
ch04.note: The source appends a biographical note to Pei Zhouyu (裹周玉), translated here: born December 1912, a native of Pingjiang, Hunan; joined the Boy Scouts in 1926 and the Communist Youth League in 1927, took part that year in the local Autumn Harvest Uprising, joined the Red Third Army Group in 1930 and the Party in 1931. He served as squad and platoon leader, divisional youth officer, inspection-section chief of the Third Army Group's security bureau, and divisional special commissioner, and took part in all four counter-encirclement campaigns of the Central Soviet and in the Long March. In the war against Japan he was security-section chief of the 358th Brigade and then of the 120th Division's political department, security head, and deputy chief of the Jin-Sui Public Security Bureau; in the civil war, director of the Suimeng Public Security Bureau and a political-department director in the First Field Army's Eighth Column. After 1949 he held senior political posts in the Volunteer Army in Korea, the 69th Army, the Beijing and Xinjiang military regions, and the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps; made a major general in 1955, he died in Beijing on June 12, 2015, aged 103.

ch04.anchor: Lieutenant General Zhao Jin'ao, to work for us
ch04.note: Zhao Jin'ao is named here as the Nationalist Yanbei (northern Shanxi) security commander whom Pei Zhouyu's network won over in 1938. The claim is the book's; independent corroboration of the name and the episode is thin, and the reading of the uncommon character 鹰 is taken from the scan.

ch04.anchor: the Japanese agents' "Kawasaki Mansion."
ch04.note: The “Kawasaki Mansion” (Chuanqi gongguan) was evidently a cover name for a Japanese special-service (tokumu) station in the Datong area; such fronts, named for their nominal proprietors, were standard Japanese intelligence practice in occupied China.

ch04.anchor: the Japanese Communist friend Okano Susumu
ch04.note: Okano Susumu was the alias under which Nosaka Sanzo (1892–1993), a founder and later chairman of the Japanese Communist Party, spent the war years in Yan'an running anti-war work among Japanese prisoners. He is introduced in Chapter 3. The source here misprints his Japanese name as 野板参三 for 野坊参三 (Nosaka).

ch04.anchor: the Department's Book-and-Press Newsletter agency
ch04.note: The Book-and-Press Newsletter (Shubao Jianxun) was the Central Intelligence Department's digest of the enemy and foreign press, compiled from the material the stations collected and circulated to the Party leadership as open-source intelligence on the enemy situation.

ch04.anchor: On April 13, 1947, Chen Yangshan gave a talk on intelligence work at the joint conference of Jin-Sui public-security chiefs. He said: "After Japan's surrender
ch04.note: This speech, dated April 13, 1947, repeats almost word for word the self-criticism the book places at a joint conference on April 13, 1948 (printed pp. 109–110). The two datings cannot both be right; the source reproduces the passage twice, under different years, without noting the discrepancy, and both are rendered here as printed.

ch04.anchor: our demolition hero Liang Shengyuan
ch04.note: Liang Shengyuan is celebrated here as the saboteur who destroyed the Taiyuan Number Two Powder Works in July 1947. The exploit is recounted a second time later in the chapter; the figures for the munitions destroyed are the book's.

ch04.anchor: into the Association for the Promotion of Democracy to carry on agent work
ch04.note: The China Association for Promoting Democracy (Zhongguo Minzhu Cujinhui), founded in Shanghai in 1945, was one of the “democratic parties” sympathetic to the Communists; the passage describes Nationalist agents trying to penetrate it, and Communist counter-intelligence exposing them.

ch04.anchor: the Twelfth Brigade commander E Yousan
ch04.note: E Yousan (1905–1951) was a Nationalist cavalry commander in Suiyuan under Fu Zuoyi, notorious for his raids into Communist territory; he refused to join Dong Qiwu's peaceful uprising in 1949, fled, and was later captured and executed.

ch04.anchor: Ma Hongkui had sent representatives to secret talks with Dong Qiwu
ch04.note: Ma Hongkui (1892–1970) was the Muslim warlord who ruled Ningxia, one of the “Ma clique” of the northwest; he pressed Dong Qiwu to keep fighting the Communists and fled to Taiwan and then the United States in 1949. Dong Qiwu (1899–1989), Fu Zuoyi's subordinate commanding in Suiyuan, instead led the peaceful “Suiyuan-way” uprising of September 1949 and served the People's Republic afterward; the intelligence his trusted men passed to Chen Yangshan's stations is described near the end of this chapter.

ch04.anchor: the Nationalist takeover officials in Beiping and Tianjin
ch04.note: The source prints “Ping-Lu” (平律) here, evidently a misprint for “Ping-Jin” (平津), the standard abbreviation for Beiping and Tianjin; the surrounding text names both cities, and the sense is followed here. The “fly-in faction” and “underground faction” were the rival cliques of returning and locally planted Nationalist officials who scrambled for the spoils of the takeover.

ch04.anchor: "Say not that the scholar only argues in the void; where the head is flung down, the blood lies in bright stains."
ch04.note: A patriotic couplet in the classical manner, honoring a scholar who dies for his cause rather than merely talking. The source opens it with 没谓 for the usual 莫谓 (“say not”); the lines circulated in the resistance period and are quoted here as the martyr Wang Shukai's epitaph.

ch04.anchor: Gao Shuxun, deputy commander-in-chief of the Nationalist Eleventh War Zone
ch04.note: Gao Shuxun's crossing-over with an army and a column at the Handan (Pinghan railway) front on October 30, 1945 was the first major Nationalist defection of the civil war and gave its name to the campaign described above. He had long been at odds with Chiang Kai-shek's central-army commanders; after 1949 he held military and civil posts under the People's Republic.

ch04.anchor: Pan Shuoduan, commander of the Nationalist 184th Division
ch04.note: Pan Shuoduan (1901–1978) led the 184th Division in revolt at Haicheng in Liaoning on May 30, 1946, the first such uprising in the Northeast; he served the People's Republic afterward as a water-conservancy and provincial official.

ch04.anchor: Captain Liu Shanben of the Nationalist air force's Eighth Flying Squadron
ch04.note: Liu Shanben (1915–1968) flew a B-24 bomber from Chengdu to Yan'an on June 26, 1946, the first Nationalist air-force pilot to defect; he became an instructor in the new People's Liberation Army air force and died during the Cultural Revolution.

ch04.anchor: a regimental commander surnamed Wei of the 320th Division of the enemy Suimeng forces led more than 1,400 men in revolt; in the spring of 1949 a battalion commander surnamed Li
ch04.note: The source withholds the given names of these two defecting Nationalist officers, printing only the surnames Wei (魔) and Li (李) followed by crosses. The redaction is the source's and is kept here.

ch04.anchor: "Let the courage be great and the heart small, the wits round and the conduct square."
ch04.note: A maxim from the Tang physician Sun Simiao (581–682), often quoted as a rule of character: be bold in daring but careful in mind, supple in wits but upright in action. The author applies it to Chen Yangshan's cast of mind.

ch04.anchor: revolutionary principle of "a needle hidden in cotton."
ch04.note: “A needle hidden in cotton” (mian li cang zhen) is a set phrase for a soft exterior over a hard, unyielding core; here it praises the tender wording but firm principle of Chen Yangshan's refusal, in the letter, to bend the marriage rule for a subordinate.

ch04.anchor: the army-organization group of the Work Committee of Yan Xishan's "Comradeship Association."
ch04.note: The Comradeship Association (Tongzhihui), fully the “Comradeship Association for the Sacrifice to Save the Nation,” was Yan Xishan's mass political organization and the instrument of his personal rule in Shanxi; its Work Committee was the inner control body. Wei Jian's rise inside it is what gave the Communist station its reach into Yan's army.

ch04.anchor: ran a "summer progressive discussion session" at Kenanpo
ch04.note: Kenanpo (“Slope of Surmounted Hardship”), in Ji County on the Yellow River in southwestern Shanxi, was Yan Xishan's wartime seat of government from 1940 after the Japanese took Taiyuan; the fortified hill complex described here ringed it.

ch04.anchor: Yan Xishan's fifth sister Yan Huiqing
ch04.note: Yan Huiqing, known as the “Fifth Miss,” was a kinswoman and confidante of Yan Xishan who managed much of his household and secretariat; she died with his regime at the fall of Taiyuan in April 1949. The book's account of her papers being rifled is the kind of hidden-front episode it favors and rests on the participants' recollections.

ch04.anchor: the Jiefang Daily printed the document in full
ch04.note: The Jiefang Daily (Liberation Daily) was the Communist Party's chief newspaper, published in Yan'an from 1941; printing the captured minutes in full was a propaganda blow against the staged Nationalist press tour.

ch04.anchor: Zhou Enlai, Marshall, and Zhang Zhizhong formed a three-man mediation group
ch04.note: The “Committee of Three” of early 1946 paired the Communist Zhou Enlai and the Nationalist Zhang Zhizhong (1890–1969), a general known for his conciliatory line who later crossed to the Communist side, with the American envoy George C. Marshall, sent by President Truman to broker a truce. The mediation collapsed into full civil war within the year.

ch04.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek's chief of the general staff Chen Cheng
ch04.note: Chen Cheng (1898–1965) was one of Chiang Kai-shek's most trusted commanders, chief of the general staff during the civil war and later premier and vice-president of the Republic of China on Taiwan; his visit to Taiyuan to whip up the war effort is the scene sketched here.

ch04.anchor: try to win a puppet National Assembly seat
ch04.note: The National Assembly (Guomin Dahui) that the Nationalists convened in November 1946, boycotted by the Communists, was denounced by them as a rubber-stamp body; hence “puppet.” A seat in it would have given the Communist agent Wu Zhezhi legal cover and access.

ch04.anchor: Wu brought 400,000 puppet fabi back from Yan'an
ch04.note: Fabi (“legal tender”) was the Nationalist paper currency; by 1945 runaway inflation had gutted its value, so a sum like 400,000 was modest working capital. The book calls it “puppet” fabi as enemy money.

ch04.anchor: copied it into an account book with a writing brush dipped in milk
ch04.note: Milk was a common improvised invisible ink: written with a brush it dries clear and shows up brown when the paper is later heated. Copying the reorganization plan this way let the agent hide it in plain sight in an ordinary ledger.

ch04.anchor: vetting work left over from the "Rescue Movement,"
ch04.note: The “Rescue Movement” (Qiangjiu yundong) of 1943 was the coercive, confession-driven phase of the Yan'an Rectification, in which many cadres were wrongly branded spies; Mao Zedong later ordered the excesses corrected. The “vetting” (zhenbie) Chen Yangshan is sent to finish was the case-by-case clearing of those wrongly accused. The movement is treated in Chapter 3.

ch04.anchor: worked his way inside the enemy secret service in Guisui
ch04.note: Guisui was the name of the city now called Hohhot, capital of Inner Mongolia; under Japanese occupation it was renamed Houhehaote. It was the seat of the Suiyuan provincial government and the focus of much of the intelligence work in this chapter (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: the Guisui Investigation and Statistics office
ch04.note: The “Investigation and Statistics” (diaotong) organs were the provincial arm of the Kuomintang party’s intelligence and counter-intelligence system, parallel to the Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong) at the center. The book uses the term for the Suiyuan provincial secret police that hunted Communist agents (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: the Chinese National Liberation Vanguard
ch04.note: A Communist-led patriotic youth organization (the “Vanguard,” Minxian) founded in Beiping in 1936; it drew students into the anti-Japanese movement and served as a recruiting ground for the Party (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: the Anwubao youth training class
ch04.note: A training school for young patriots run at Anwubao, in Jingyang County, Shaanxi, on the edge of the Communist border region; nominally a Nationalist youth camp, it was in practice a Communist cadre school in the late 1930s (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: the Sacrifice League
ch04.note: The Shanxi Sacrifice for National Salvation League (Xisheng jiuguo tongmenghui, or Ximeng Hui), a mass anti-Japanese body set up under Yan Xishan in 1936 but heavily penetrated and led by Communists (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: In 1912 the Central Organization Department
ch04.note: So printed; plainly a misprint for 1942. The training class at Zaoyuan in Yan’an belongs to the 1940s, and the narrative has just placed Zhang He in the Shaan-Gan-Ning region in 1941 (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: good-citizen certificate
ch04.note: The liangmin zheng, an identity pass issued to civilians in Japanese-occupied areas; carrying a proper one was essential to move through checkpoints (printed folio 137).

ch04.anchor: the puppet Houhehaote city post office
ch04.note: Houhehaote (from the Mongolian name of the city) was the name imposed on Guisui under the Japanese-sponsored Mongol regime; “puppet” marks the occupation administration (printed folio 137).

ch04.anchor: During the First Suiyuan Campaign in November 1945
ch04.note: The Communist offensive of October–December 1945 that besieged Guisui and Baotou in the opening months of the civil war; it failed to take either city (printed folio 138).

ch04.anchor: the security system of the Jin-Ji district of Jin-Cha-Ji
ch04.note: Jin-Cha-Ji (Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei) was one of the great Communist base areas of north China; “Jin-Ji” denotes its Shanxi-Hebei sub-region (printed folio 138).

ch04.anchor: the Resource Investigation Society
ch04.note: A Japanese secret-service organ operating under an economic-survey cover in occupied Shanxi; after the surrender Yan Xishan took it over, keeping some of its Japanese staff (printed folio 141).

ch04.anchor: he wrote to Gao Kelin
ch04.note: Gao Kelin (1907–1989), a veteran Communist then heading the Party’s Saibei district committee and its Social Affairs Department (intelligence and security); later a senior judicial official of the People’s Republic (printed folio 139).

ch04.anchor: The director of the Yanbei office was Chu Xichun
ch04.note: Chu Xichun (1896–1966), a Yan Xishan general who in 1949 took part in the peaceful handover of Beiping and served the People’s Republic thereafter (printed folio 141).

ch04.anchor: the Ministry of State Security set up a leading group
ch04.note: The PRC Ministry of State Security, formed in 1983 by merging the counter-intelligence work of the Ministry of Public Security with the Party’s Investigation Department; in 1985 it gathered veterans like Chen Yangshan to record the history of the hidden front (printed folio 142).

ch04.anchor: Comrade Lu Nan
ch04.note: Lu Nan was the codename of Zhao Xihong (also called Zhao Fumin), the agent whose network this section follows; the name echoes his Shandong birthplace (Lu is the classical name for Shandong). He is not to be confused with the southern-Shandong region (printed folio 143).

ch04.anchor: He Shaonan's security-command headquarters at Suide
ch04.note: He Shaonan was the Kuomintang commissioner and security commander of the Suide district on the Shaan-Gan-Ning border; his clashes with the Communists ended when he was driven out in 1940 (printed folio 143).

ch04.anchor: the garrison commander Chen Qihan
ch04.note: Chen Qihan (1897–1981), a senior Red Army and later PLA commander, made a general in 1955 and president of the PLA Military Court (printed folio 143).

ch04.anchor: the Ike Zhao League of Suiyuan province
ch04.note: The Ike Zhao League (Yeke Juu) was the Mongol banner-league of the Ordos region, in the great southern bend of the Yellow River; it is now the city of Ordos (printed folio 143).

ch04.anchor: Ma Zhanshan's force
ch04.note: Ma Zhanshan (1885–1950), the general famed for defying orders and fighting the Japanese in Manchuria in 1931–32; by this time he commanded cavalry in the northwest (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: the third class of the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University
ch04.note: The Anti-Japanese Military and Political University (Kangda), the Communists’ chief training academy at Yan’an, which turned out military and political cadres in successive classes through the war (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: Here were Chen Changjie's Ike Zhao League Garrison Command
ch04.note: Chen Changjie (1892–1968), a Yan Xishan and later Nationalist general; he commanded the defense of Tianjin and was captured when the city fell in January 1949 (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: of the Juntong system
ch04.note: Juntong (the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission) was the Nationalists’ military secret service under Dai Li, distinct from the party’s Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong); the rivalry between the two runs through this section. After 1946 Juntong was reorganized as the Bureau of Confidential Investigation (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: On the eve of the Party's Seventh Congress in 1945
ch04.note: The Chinese Communist Party’s Seventh National Congress, held at Yan’an from April to June 1945, which enshrined Mao Zedong Thought and set the line for the final drive to power (printed folio 145).

ch04.anchor: to rail at Ma Hansan
ch04.note: Ma Hansan, the Juntong chief in the northwest, was himself arrested and shot by his own service in 1948 for embezzlement, including the theft of a jeweled Qing seal; the source elsewhere spells his name Ma Hanshan (printed folio 145).

ch04.anchor: an introductory document signed by Ouyang Qin
ch04.note: Ouyang Qin (1900–1978), a senior Communist then in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Security Office, later first Party secretary of Heilongjiang (printed folio 146).

ch04.anchor: to defect through contact with Dong Qiwu
ch04.note: The source appends a biographical footnote here: Dong Qiwu (1899–1989) joined the army in 1919 and served through the Northern Expedition; from 1928 he rose under Fu Zuoyi as staff officer, regimental and brigade commander; he fought at the Great Wall in 1933 and helped organize the 1936 Suiyuan resistance. In 1949 he led the Suiyuan peaceful uprising; in 1951 he commanded the 23rd Corps of the Chinese People’s Volunteers in Korea, and in 1955 was made a general. He joined the Communist Party in 1980 and died in 1989 (printed folio 148).

ch04.anchor: the "Suiyuan formula,"
ch04.note: The Suiyuan fangshi, the Party’s policy of leaving Suiyuan’s Nationalist forces in place under a standing truce until they could be brought over peacefully rather than crushed; it produced Dong Qiwu’s bloodless uprising of September 1949 (printed folio 148).

ch04.anchor: the collaborator Zhou Fohai's
ch04.note: Zhou Fohai (1897–1948), a founder of the Communist Party who defected to the Kuomintang and then became a leading minister in Wang Jingwei’s Japanese-sponsored government; he died in prison after the war (printed folio 151).

ch04.anchor: and Chen Gongbo's
ch04.note: Chen Gongbo (1892–1946), another founding Communist turned Nationalist, who succeeded Wang Jingwei as head of the puppet regime at Nanjing; he was tried and executed in 1946 (printed folio 151).

ch04.anchor: After the Shangdang Campaign of January 1945
ch04.note: So dated in the source, but in error: the Shangdang Campaign, in which Yan Xishan lost some thirteen divisions, was fought in September and October 1945. The reorganization it forced is the same one described in section 4 (printed folio 153).

ch04.anchor: an army doctor in He Zhuguo's 2nd Cavalry Army
ch04.note: He Zhuguo (1897–1985), a cavalry general of the Northeastern Army; naming him lent Zheng Gui’s cover story a plausible wartime record (printed folio 156).

ch04.anchor: deep-cover funds from Mao Renfeng
ch04.note: Mao Renfeng (1898–1956), who took over the Nationalist secret service after Dai Li’s death in 1946 and ran the Bureau of Confidential Investigation through the civil war (printed folio 158).

ch04.anchor: hand out the gold-yuan notes
ch04.note: The gold yuan (jinyuan quan), the currency the Nationalist government issued in August 1948 to replace the collapsing fabi; it too collapsed within months in runaway inflation (printed folio 158).

ch04.anchor: the North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters
ch04.note: The jiaozong, the Nationalist regional command charged with “suppressing bandits,” their term for the Communists; the North China headquarters under Fu Zuoyi directed the defense of the Beiping-Tianjin region (printed folio 158).

ch04.anchor: from the September 19 Suiyuan uprising
ch04.note: On September 19, 1949, Dong Qiwu led the Nationalist forces and administration of Suiyuan to defect to the Communists without a fight, the culmination of the “Suiyuan formula” (printed folio 160).

ch04.anchor: the Pinggui line (the Datong-Jining section) and the Tongpu Railway
ch04.note: Two rail lines that framed the region. The Pinggui line is the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway (平绥), whose western reach—the Datong–Jining section—ran along the region’s northeastern edge; it is the same line the book later calls the Ping-Sui Railway. The Tongpu Railway (同蒲) ran the length of Shanxi north to south, from Datong down to Puzhou on the Yellow River. Control of both was contested throughout.

ch04.anchor: running through Baotou, Bailingmiao, Wuchuan
ch04.note: Baotou (包头), the westernmost major city of Suiyuan (now in Inner Mongolia), an industrial and trading town on the north bank of the Yellow River; with Guisui it was a chief Nationalist-held objective in the region. Bailingmiao (Bat Khaalga), to its north, had been the site of a noted 1936 battle against Japanese-backed Mongol forces.

ch04.anchor: the international route to Outer Mongolia and the Soviet Union
ch04.note: Outer Mongolia here means the Mongolian People’s Republic, the Soviet-aligned state on China’s northern border; because it opened onto the USSR, it offered the Communist base areas a potential back-door land route to Soviet territory and aid.

ch04.anchor: the Center set up a Jin-Sui Sub-bureau there especially
ch04.note: The CCP Jin-Sui Sub-bureau (晋绥分局), the Party’s top regional organ for the Shanxi-Suiyuan base area, subordinate to the Central Committee; it directed the region’s Party, government, and intelligence work.

ch04.anchor: When Chiang Kai-shek launched his third anti-Communist upsurge
ch04.note: During the wartime united front the Nationalists mounted three “anti-Communist upsurges” (反共高潮), military-political drives against the CCP, in 1939–40, 1940–41, and 1943. The third coincided with Hu Zongnan’s forces massing to threaten Yan’an, which the passage refers to as his 1947 raid.

ch04.anchor: namely Taiyuan, Datong, Guisui
ch04.note: Taiyuan (太原), the capital of Shanxi and Yan Xishan’s fortified stronghold; the largest enemy-held city in the region and the focus of much of the intelligence work described here. It fell to the Communists only in April 1949.

ch04.anchor: Baotou, and Yulin
ch04.note: Yulin (榆林), a walled garrison city in the far north of Shaanxi, held by the Nationalists through the civil war and a watch-post for intelligence toward the northwest.

ch04.anchor: Xi'an, Shijiazhuang, Beiping, Tianjin
ch04.note: Shijiazhuang (石家庄), also called Shimen, a railway-junction city in Hebei where the Peiping–Wuhan and Zhengding–Taiyuan lines crossed; the Communists took it in November 1947, their first capture of a sizable city.

ch04.anchor: member of the CCP Northwest Bureau and head of its Social Affairs Department
ch04.note: The CCP Northwest Bureau (西北局), the Party’s top regional bureau for the northwest, overseeing the Shaan-Gan-Ning and Jin-Sui base areas from Yan’an.

ch04.anchor: Feng Jiping, Liang Hanbing, and others
ch04.note: Feng Jiping (冯基平, 1911–1983), a Communist intelligence and security cadre sent to strengthen the Jin-Sui bureau; after 1949 he became chief of the Beijing Public Security Bureau.

ch04.anchor: and on through Suide to Yan'an
ch04.note: Suide (绑德), a prefectural town in northern Shaanxi on the road between the Jin-Sui base and Yan’an; it was the transit point through which books, papers, and intelligence passed to the Party Center.

ch04.anchor: the Xing County dormant cell of the puppet Juntong's
ch04.note: Xing County (Xingxian, 兴县), in the hills of northwestern Shanxi, was the seat of the Jin-Sui Border Region government—the “capital” the book refers to below.

ch04.anchor: the Social Affairs Department of the North China Bureau, which won commendation
ch04.note: The CCP North China Bureau (华北局), the Party’s regional bureau for north China; its Social Affairs Department ran the region’s intelligence and security work.

ch04.anchor: Jin-Cha-Ji and Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu are to be merged
ch04.note: The Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu (Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan, 晋冊鲁豫) base area, a large Communist base on the north China plain, is here being joined with the neighboring Jin-Cha-Ji base to unify the work; their merger in 1948 formed the North China base area.

ch04.anchor: the former Taiyue District south of Hongzhao
ch04.note: Taiyue (太岳), the mountain sub-region of south-central Shanxi around the Taiyue range, one of the districts of the Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu base area.

ch04.anchor: the key Jinnan town of Linfen
ch04.note: Linfen (临汶), the chief city of “Jinnan” (southern Shanxi); the People’s Liberation Army took it in May 1948 after a long and costly siege, opening all of southern Shanxi.

ch04.anchor: to support the Jinzhong Campaign
ch04.note: The Jinzhong (central-Shanxi) Campaign of June–July 1948, in which Xu Xiangqian’s outnumbered forces destroyed some 100,000 of Yan Xishan’s troops on the plain around Taiyuan, isolating the city for its final siege.

ch04.anchor: where Feng Jinchen conveyed the higher-level instructions
ch04.note: Feng Jinchen (冯晋場), deputy chief of the communications section of Chen Yangshan’s bureau; one of the three subordinates to whom Chen’s secret letter (Section 4) is addressed.

ch04.anchor: He Long had once been commander of the Nationalist Twentieth Army
ch04.note: He Long commanded the National Revolutionary Army’s Twentieth Army (第二十军), which he led into the Communist-organized Nanchang Uprising of August 1, 1927.

ch04.anchor: deputy director Zou Dapeng had already returned to Yan'an
ch04.note: Zou Dapeng (邹大鹏, 1907–1967), a leading Communist intelligence officer who had run the Jin-Sui Investigation Bureau before Chen Yangshan; he went on to build the Party’s intelligence network in the Northeast and, after 1949, to head its central investigation apparatus. He and his wife were driven to suicide in the Cultural Revolution. (The former director Zhou Yi, named alongside him, is little documented outside this account.)

ch04.anchor: In the vetting of Wang Shukai, for instance
ch04.note: Wang Shukai, a Jin-Sui intelligence cadre, cleared here in the vetting; later reconnaissance-section chief of the Suimeng Public Security Bureau and head of the Youyu station. He fell in battle at Cai’erying east of Youyu in May 1947 and was beheaded by the enemy; the book honors him below as a hero of the hidden front.

ch04.anchor: winning over the enemy's Yanbei security commander
ch04.note: Yanbei (雅北, “north of the pass”), the region of far-northern Shanxi beyond Yanmen Pass, centered on Datong.

ch04.anchor: Lan County Gendarmerie Special-Work Team
ch04.note: Lan County (Lanxian, 嵐县) lies in the mountains of northwestern Shanxi; the “special-work team” (tokumu) was a Japanese military-intelligence and gendarmerie detachment of the kind planted in occupied towns. Lanxian is the setting of one of the tales in Section 8.

ch04.anchor: the organization and activity of the Special Police and Gendarmerie Command
ch04.note: The Special Police and Gendarmerie Command (特警宪兵指挥部), one of Yan Xishan’s secret-police organs in Taiyuan; the book describes it below, formed from his mobile agent teams under Liang Huazhi and Xu Duan.

ch04.anchor: In the Qingfengdian Campaign our Beiping inside-line connections
ch04.note: The Qingfengdian Campaign of October 1947, near Dingzhou in Hebei, in which Yang Dezhi’s Jin-Cha-Ji forces destroyed the Nationalist Third Army (第三军) and captured its commander Luo Lirong, clearing the way to take Shijiazhuang.

ch04.anchor: pamphlet What Is the Pacification Intensification Movement
ch04.note: The pamphlet analyzes the Japanese “Campaign to Strengthen Public Order” (治安强化运动), a series of five drives across occupied north China in 1941–42 that combined blockade lines, population control, and “mopping-up” sweeps to consolidate the occupation.

ch04.anchor: praising the work in Suimeng, the Eighth Sub-bureau
ch04.note: Sui-Meng, or Suimeng (绑蒙), the Suiyuan-Mongol border sub-region on the northwestern edge of the Jin-Sui base area; its public-security bureau and stations recur throughout what follows.

ch04.anchor: the Second Department of the Ministry of National Defense
ch04.note: The Second Department of the Ministry of National Defense (国防部第二厅) was the Nationalist military’s intelligence department; the Bureau of Confidential Investigation (Baomiju) operated under it.

ch04.anchor: the puppet Thirty-eighth Division
ch04.note: The Thirty-eighth Division (第三十八师), a Yan Xishan formation—raised partly from surrendered puppet troops—that garrisoned Datong; its later commander was Han Buzhou. The Datong network obtained its order of battle and the city’s defense plans.

ch04.anchor: the 111th, 158th, and 320th Divisions and the 13th Cavalry Brigade
ch04.note: Main Nationalist forces under Fu Zuoyi in the Suiyuan-Baotou area. The unit numbers are load-bearing: the 320th Division reappears below, its 959th Regiment (under Wei Gang) being brought over to the Communists in May 1949.

ch04.anchor: Wang Qian, Jinchen, Xiaoxian
ch04.note: Wang Qian (王谦, 1917–2007), a Shanxi Communist and one of Chen Yangshan’s subordinates addressed in this letter; decades later he became first Party secretary of Shanxi province and, later still, Party secretary of Sichuan.

ch04.anchor: The last letter from Comrade Xinfu
ch04.note: “Xinfu” is the working name of Zhang Xinfu, who also used the cover name Li Wenfang; the Jin-Sui courier sent to lead the Taiyuan station. His exposure wrecked the station, and—believing he had failed the Party—he took his own life, as the full account in Section 4 relates.

ch04.anchor: what Wang Lianzhong and the Zhou brothers have told
ch04.note: Wang Lianzhong was the working name of Cui Shou’an, a courier of the Taiyuan station. When the station was betrayed he was seized and, giving up nothing under torture, died in the enemy’s hands. (The “Zhou brothers” were Zhou Peiji and his kin, also of the station.)

ch04.anchor: Feng Jinchen, and Zheng Xiaoxian
ch04.note: Zheng Xiaoxian, a Jin-Sui intelligence officer (head of the Yangqu station, later intelligence-section chief of the Sui-Meng Public Security Bureau); his memoirs are among the book’s sources for this chapter, including the tales in Section 8.

ch04.anchor: In early 1941 Wei Jian and the other intelligence workers
ch04.note: Wei Jian, the Communist agent who is the central figure of this section: working inside Yan Xishan’s own apparatus at Taiyuan, he rose through its ranks to colonel-grade posts in the “Comradeship Association” and fed out military and organizational intelligence for years.

ch04.anchor: the Eighth Route Army's Shanxi liaison office at Qiulin
ch04.note: Qiulin (秋林), a town in Yichuan County on the Yellow River where Yan Xishan kept his wartime headquarters after retreating from Taiyuan; the Eighth Route Army maintained a liaison office there during the united front.

ch04.anchor: Its main members were Wu Peishen
ch04.note: Wu Peishen, a member of the Taiyuan intelligence group and its link to the Eighth Route Army’s Qiulin office; in 1945 he made his way to Yan’an, reported the group’s work to Li Kenong, and carried the Center’s instructions back.

ch04.anchor: an editor at the National Revolution News Agency
ch04.note: The National Revolution News Agency (民族革命通讯社), the press organ of Yan Xishan’s “National Revolution” apparatus; a reporter’s cover let Communist agents move about and gather information.

ch04.anchor: Zhang Lixian, then a reporter at the same agency
ch04.note: Zhang Lixian, a member of the group working under cover as a reporter at Yan Xishan’s news agency; he is celebrated below for stealing, and swiftly copying, the secret record of the 1944 anti-Communist talks between Yan and the Nationalist “observation group.”

ch04.anchor: the Central News Agency, the Central Daily, the Saodang Bao
ch04.note: Two more Nationalist papers alongside the official wire service: the Central Daily (中央日报), the Kuomintang’s flagship organ, and the Saodang Bao (扫荡报, “Mopping-Up News”), the paper of the Nationalist armed forces.

ch04.anchor: Chinese and Foreign Reporters' Northwest Observation Group
ch04.note: A party of Chinese and Western journalists whom the Nationalist government, under Allied pressure, allowed to tour the northwest in the spring of 1944, reaching Yan’an in May–June (their visit preceded the U.S. Army’s “Dixie Mission”). The book charges that Chiang planted CC-Clique agents among them.

ch04.anchor: Wang Jingguo's Iron Army group, Liang Huazhi's literati group
ch04.note: The rival cliques among Yan Xishan’s senior men. Wang Jingguo (王靖国) was Yan’s foremost field general; Liang Huazhi (梁化之, also Liang Dunhou), a kinsman by marriage, ran Yan’s secret police and killed himself when Taiyuan fell in 1949. The others named led lesser factions.

ch04.anchor: made "progress-guarantee commissioner
ch04.note: “Progress-guarantee commissioner” (进步保证委员) was a post in Yan Xishan’s peculiar apparatus of ideological control, charged with vouching for and policing the political “progress” of officers and men.

ch04.anchor: the deputy commander-in-chief Yang Aiyuan
ch04.note: Yang Aiyuan (杨爱源, 1886–1959), a Baoding-trained general and one of Yan Xishan’s most senior commanders, latterly his deputy at the Taiyuan Pacification Office; he followed Yan to Taiwan.

ch04.anchor: our Eighteenth Group Army's Qiulin liaison office
ch04.note: The Eighth Route Army’s formal designation in the Nationalist order of battle was the Eighteenth Group Army (第十八集团军); the book uses the two names interchangeably.

ch04.anchor: the Taiyue Third Prefectural Committee secretary Chai Zemin
ch04.note: Chai Zemin (柴泽民, 1916–2010), a Shanxi Communist named here as a local Party secretary; decades later he became the People’s Republic’s first ambassador to the United States (1979–82).

ch04.anchor: the home of Wei Jian's younger brother Zhou Peiji
ch04.note: Zhou Peiji, Wei Jian’s younger clansman and a communications helper of the Taiyuan station. Arrested in 1947 while escorting Wei Jian’s wife and children out of the city, he was buried alive by Yan Xishan’s men on the eve of Taiyuan’s liberation.

ch04.anchor: a missing-person notice for a week in Yan Xishan's Fuxing Daily
ch04.note: The Fuxing Ribao (复兴日报, “Renaissance Daily”), one of Yan Xishan’s Taiyuan newspapers; a coded personal notice in its columns served as the agents’ pre-arranged contact signal.

ch04.anchor: Zhang He, who took the name Zhang Youxin after Liberation
ch04.note: Zhang He (later Zhang Youxin), a native of Youyu County in Shanxi and a Communist agent trained in cryptography, who twice worked his way into the Nationalist secret service at Guisui; the subject of this section.

ch04.anchor: set out from Pianguan with Zhang Dazhi's cavalry brigade
ch04.note: Zhang Dazhi (张达志, 1911–1992), a founder of the north-Shaanxi Red base and commander of the 120th Division’s Daqingshan cavalry detachment; later a lieutenant general of the PLA and commander of the Lanzhou Military Region.

ch04.anchor: Building the Datong Intelligence Network
ch04.note: Datong (大同), the great coal city of far-northern Shanxi and a rail junction on the Ping-Sui and Tongpu lines; held first by the Japanese and then by Yan Xishan, it was a principal target of the intelligence work in this and the neighboring sections.

ch04.anchor: Fang Shaoming was one of the outstanding ones
ch04.note: Fang Shaoming, cover name of Wang Yanming (王弹明), a former Long March soldier who—after leaving the ranks and being captured by the Japanese—became the Communists’ chief agent in the Datong area; his story fills this section.

ch04.anchor: the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army
ch04.note: The Eighth Route Army’s 120th Division, commanded by He Long, operated in northwestern Shanxi and pushed into the Daqingshan; it was the military backbone of the Jin-Sui base area.

ch04.anchor: were Cui Jizhou and Gong Zhen
ch04.note: Cui Jizhou, an agent first developed and run by Lu Nan. Posing as a servant and errand-boy, he penetrated Nationalist offices across Suiyuan and, after Lu Nan’s death, helped carry the network through to the peaceful liberation of Suiyuan.

ch04.anchor: the anti-smuggling office of the Eighth War Zone
ch04.note: The Eighth War Zone (第八战区), the Nationalist theater command for the northwest (Gansu, Ningxia, Suiyuan), under Zhu Shaoliang with Fu Zuoyi as deputy; its anti-smuggling office doubled as a cover for Juntong intelligence.

ch04.anchor: Zhang Qing'en, chief of the Suiyuan Investigation and Statistics secret service
ch04.note: Zhang Qing’en, director of the Nationalist Investigation-and-Statistics (Zhongtong) secret service in Suiyuan and secretary-general of the province’s Kuomintang party office. He fled by air to Taiwan in September 1949 as Suiyuan went over to the Communists.

ch04.anchor: In mid-October 1948, during the Cha-Sui Campaign
ch04.note: The Cha-Sui (Chahar-Suiyuan) Campaign of autumn 1948, a Communist offensive that tied down Fu Zuoyi’s forces in the west; as the book explains, its purpose was to keep Fu from reinforcing the Northeast during the decisive Liaoshen battle.

ch04.anchor: the decisive battle of Liaoshen
ch04.note: The Liaoshen (Liao-Shen) Campaign, September to November 1948, the first of the three great decisive campaigns of the civil war, in which the People’s Liberation Army destroyed the Nationalists’ forces in the Northeast and won all of Manchuria.

ch04.anchor: first wiped out Fu's main-force 35th Army at Xinbao'an
ch04.note: The Battle of Xinbao’an, December 1948, the opening blow of the Pingjin (Beiping-Tianjin) Campaign: the PLA annihilated Fu Zuoyi’s crack 35th Army (第三十五军)—its commander Guo Jingyu killed himself—clearing the way for the peaceful surrender of Beiping.

ch04.anchor: from Baotou to the Hetao
ch04.note: The Hetao (河套, “River Loop”), the irrigated plain within the great northern bend of the Yellow River in western Suiyuan; the last redoubt to which the Nationalist secret service withdrew.

ch04.anchor: such papers and magazines as the Mainichi and the Yomiuri
ch04.note: The Mainichi Shimbun and the Yomiuri Shimbun, two of Japan’s largest national daily newspapers; the station subscribed to them for the Party Center’s study of the enemy.

ch04.anchor: a Japanese-run kabushiki company
ch04.note: “Kabushiki” is Japanese for shares or stock; a kabushiki-gaisha (株式会社) is a joint-stock company—here a Japanese-run firm in occupied Taiyuan.

ch04.anchor: a "tongue" who could give a full account
ch04.note: In Chinese (and Soviet) military usage a “tongue” (舌头) is a live prisoner seized expressly to be interrogated—a captive taken for the intelligence he carries.

ch04.anchor: the man of the first merit was Zheng Gui
ch04.note: Zheng Gui, a Datong-born Communist agent—a country doctor by cover—who penetrated the Nationalist Bureau of Confidential Investigation’s Suiyuan station and turned two of its officers; the subject of this final tale.

ch04.anchor: Xing Shaowen, was a sworn brother of Zheng Gui's
ch04.note: Xing Shaowen, an officer of the Nationalist Bureau of Confidential Investigation’s Suiyuan station and Zheng Gui’s boyhood sworn brother; won over by Zheng, he became a key source and helped destroy the Suiyuan secret service from within.

ch04.anchor: Pang Zhongxing, head of the enemy Bureau of Confidential Investigation's Suiyuan station
ch04.note: Pang Zhongxing, chief of the Nationalist Bureau of Confidential Investigation’s Suiyuan station until he was dismissed for corruption in the spring of 1949.

ch04.anchor: introduced Wu Yumei to Zheng Gui
ch04.note: Wu Yumei, a senior Suiyuan Juntong officer—chief adjutant of the 12th Reorganized Cavalry Brigade—who held the service’s internal files. Turned by Zheng Gui at the eleventh hour, he handed the files over, breaking the Suiyuan network.

ch05.anchor: come at once to Beiping for the First National Public Security Work Conference
ch05.note: The First National Public Security Work Conference, held in Beijing in the autumn of 1949, set the framework for the new state's security organs. (Beiping was the name of the city until it was renamed Beijing in October 1949; the source uses both.)

ch05.anchor: put up at the Six Nations Hotel on Zhengyi Road
ch05.note: The Six Nations Hotel (the Grand Hotel des Wagons-Lits) stood in the old Legation Quarter of Beijing and had long been a place where foreigners and Chinese officials met.

ch05.anchor: Our 'lucky general' is here
ch05.note: “Lucky general” (fujiang) is an affectionate term for a commander under whom things always seem to go well; Li Kenong uses it warmly of Chen Yangshan.

ch05.anchor: Luo Ruiqing to chief of the Beiping bureau
ch05.note: Luo Ruiqing (1906-1978) became the first Minister of Public Security of the People's Republic and later PLA chief of staff; he was purged in 1966 and rehabilitated after his death.

ch05.anchor: his wife, Zhang Suzhen, back to their home district
ch05.note: Zhang Suzhen was Chen Yangshan's wife.

ch05.anchor: the "sacred ground of six dynasties"
ch05.note: Nanjing served as capital of a succession of dynasties from the third to the sixth century (the “Six Dynasties”), and again under the Ming and the Republic; hence its reputation as an imperial city.

ch05.anchor: a veteran secret agent and traitor of the Kuomintang's Central Statistics Bureau
ch05.note: The Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong) was the Kuomintang party's civilian intelligence and secret-police organ, distinct from the military Juntong; it is a recurring adversary in this book.

ch05.anchor: Our Party's Central Committee member Yang Pao'an
ch05.note: Yang Pao'an (1896-1931) was one of the earliest Chinese Marxist writers; he was arrested and executed in Shanghai in 1931. His fellow martyr Luo Qiyuan (1894-1931), a leader of the peasant movement, died at the same time.

ch05.anchor: the patriot Deng Yanda
ch05.note: Deng Yanda (1895-1931), a leader of the Kuomintang left and founder of the “Third Party,” was secretly executed on Chiang Kai-shek's order in November 1931.

ch05.anchor: impersonated Wu Hao, Zhou Enlai's alias, to run a "Wu Hao Notice"
ch05.note: “Wu Hao” was a pen name Zhou Enlai had used since his student days. In 1932 the Kuomintang forged a notice in which “Wu Hao and 243 others” announced their withdrawal from the Communist Party, to discredit Zhou; the fabrication and its rebuttal are the subject of the pages that follow. The story is well documented and forms a set piece of Party history.

ch05.anchor: together with another Central Statistics agent, Zhang Chong
ch05.note: Zhang Chong (1904-1941) was a Kuomintang Central Statistics figure who took part in the anti-Communist forgeries but later, as a liaison for Kuomintang-Communist cooperation, earned the respect of Zhou Enlai and others.

ch05.anchor: only four members of the Party's Central Politburo remained in Shanghai
ch05.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880-1931), a former worker, was the nominal general secretary of the Party from 1928. Arrested in Shanghai in June 1931, he defected on the spot but was executed by the Kuomintang within days.

ch05.anchor: Zhou Enlai moved swiftly to the Metropole Hotel on Simalu
ch05.note: Simalu (“Fourth Avenue”) is the old name of Fuzhou Road in Shanghai; the Metropole was a foreign-run hotel, chosen because the concession authorities limited Kuomintang police action there.

ch05.anchor: Xiang Zhongfa gave up Ren Bishi's wife, Chen Congying
ch05.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950) was a top Party leader; his wife Chen Congying, herself a veteran underground worker, was arrested in this sweep but gave nothing away under torture.

ch05.anchor: On the proposal of the Comintern's Far Eastern Bureau
ch05.note: The Communist International (Comintern) directed the Chinese Party through its Far Eastern Bureau; the provisional Politburo it approved was dominated by the Moscow-trained group around Bo Gu.

ch05.anchor: made up of six men — Bo Gu, Zhang Wentian
ch05.note: Bo Gu (Qin Bangxian, 1907-1946) and Zhang Wentian (1900-1976) were leading figures of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-Eight Bolsheviks”; Bo Gu was de facto Party leader until the 1935 Zunyi Conference. Lu Futan and Li Zhusheng, also named here, both later defected to the Kuomintang after arrest.

ch05.anchor: He had used it for a long time
ch05.note: The Awakening (Juewu) was a progressive newspaper supplement associated with Zhou Enlai's Awakening Society in Tianjin around 1919-1920.

ch05.anchor: issue a statement in the Party Central organ Struggle
ch05.note: Struggle (Douzheng) was an organ of the Party Central Committee in the early 1930s.

ch05.anchor: chairman of the provisional central government of the Chinese Soviet Republic
ch05.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic, proclaimed in the Jiangxi base area in November 1931 with Mao Zedong as chairman, gave the Communists a rival government to the Nationalist state.

ch05.anchor: Mr. Tao Xingzhi, a democratic figure serving as adviser to the Shen Bao
ch05.note: Tao Xingzhi (1891-1946) was a celebrated progressive educator; the Shen Bao (Shanghai News) was the most influential newspaper of the Republican era.

ch05.anchor: he would go to its chairman, Shi Liangcai
ch05.note: Shi Liangcai (1880-1934), owner of the Shen Bao, backed resistance to Japan and civil rights; Kuomintang agents assassinated him in 1934. The account of his reluctance here fits his known independence, though the private exchanges the author reports cannot be independently verified.

ch05.anchor: the licensed French lawyer Ba He
ch05.note: The source names the French lawyer only in Chinese transcription (Ba He); histories of the episode identify the rebuttal notice as issued through a French lawyer in the Shanghai concessions, whose extraterritorial standing put him beyond Kuomintang reprisal. The underlying French name is not established here.

ch05.anchor: winning over Wang Yaqiao, the foremost assassin of the Republic
ch05.note: Wang Yaqiao (1889-1936) led a famous band of assassins in Republican Shanghai and mounted attempts on Chiang Kai-shek and others; the Communist underground cultivated ties with him. He was himself assassinated by Kuomintang agents in 1936.

ch05.anchor: the Panmunjom talks during the War to Resist America and Aid Korea
ch05.note: Li Kenong headed the Chinese side's work at the Korean armistice negotiations at Panmunjom (1951-1953); “the War to Resist America and Aid Korea” is China's name for its part in the Korean War.

ch05.anchor: When the American Central Intelligence Agency learned of his death
ch05.note: This often-repeated claim, that the CIA declared a holiday when Li Kenong died in 1962, circulates widely in Chinese accounts of him but rests on no verifiable source and is best read as legend rather than fact.

ch05.anchor: he put on the gleaming rank of a colonel general
ch05.note: In the People's Liberation Army's first system of ranks (1955), shangjiang corresponds to colonel general (three-star). The three orders named — of August the First, of Independence and Freedom, of Liberation — honored, respectively, service in the founding of the Red Army, the war against Japan, and the war of liberation.

ch05.anchor: he served as executive head of the State Political Security Bureau
ch05.note: The State Political Security Bureau was the security and intelligence organ of the Chinese Soviet Republic, set up in 1931.

ch05.anchor: settling the screening left over from the
