ch05.note: The “Rescue” campaign of 1943, an offshoot of the Yan'an Rectification run by Kang Sheng, extracted many false confessions of espionage; the “screening” (zhenbie) that followed was the work of clearing the wrongly accused.

ch05.anchor: a villa on Yueyang Road that had once been Kong Xiangxi's
ch05.note: Kong Xiangxi (1881-1967), known in the West as H. H. Kung, was a financier and premier of Nationalist China and one of its richest men; his former Shanghai residences passed to the state after 1949.

ch05.anchor: Li Kenong's "conscientious and responsible resolving" of the political question of Xu Qiang
ch05.note: Xu Qiang, a veteran of the Central Special Branch, had been imprisoned in Yan'an on Kang Sheng's order without evidence; Li Kenong personally revised the finding to clear him.

ch05.anchor: swept the graves of Peng Pai, Lü Ming, Li Bai
ch05.note: Li Bai (1910-1949) was the Communist underground radio operator executed in Shanghai on the eve of liberation, later famous through the film The Unfailing Radio Waves; he is not the Tang poet of the same name. Peng Pai (1896-1929) was the pioneer of the Communist peasant movement, executed in Shanghai.

ch05.anchor: The Campaign to Suppress Counter-Revolutionaries launched across the country in 1951
ch05.note: This nationwide campaign of 1950-1951 struck at former Kuomintang agents, secret-society heads, and other opponents of the new order, with mass rallies and many executions; the debate over a “steady” versus a “bold and open” line was a real policy question of the day.

ch05.anchor: The party secretary, Ke Qingshi
ch05.note: Ke Qingshi (1902-1965), then Nanjing party secretary, later became mayor of Shanghai and a Politburo member known for his radical leftism.

ch05.anchor: During the "Three-Antis" campaign of 1951
ch05.note: The “Three-Antis” campaign (1951-1952) targeted corruption, waste, and bureaucratism among officials; the quota-setting the passage criticizes was a common abuse of such mass campaigns.

ch05.anchor: a magazine called Celebrity Biography, published by a press in Zhengzhou
ch05.note: The episode concerns a piece of popular reportage the author regarded as plagiarized from Mu Xin's biography General Chen Geng and padded with invention; Mu Xin (1920-2010) was a journalist and Party historian. The author's own book is thus in part a corrective to such embroidered accounts of the intelligence war.

ch05.anchor: at a meeting of the leading members of the Supreme People's Procuratorate
ch05.note: The Supreme People's Procuratorate is the state's highest organ of legal supervision and prosecution; Chen Yangshan served in the procuratorial system in his later years.

ch05.anchor: In 1935, Chen Yangshan had done underground work in Chongqing and Chengdu with Chen Chang
ch05.note: Chen Chang, wrongly branded a suspected agent after liberation and hounded to his death in 1960, was posthumously cleared in 1961 largely through Chen Yangshan's efforts — even as Chen Yangshan himself was under attack, a foretaste of the persecution recounted in the next chapter.

ch05.anchor: the leader who had sent them to Sichuan in those years
ch05.note: Wang Shiying (1905-1968), a veteran of Communist intelligence and united-front work, had directed underground operations in the southwest.

ch05.anchor: the "anti-Party clique" case of the Ministry of Justice's Party group had been reviewed by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection
ch05.note: In 1958 Chen Yangshan was caught up, with others of the Ministry of Justice's Party group, in a fabricated “anti-Party clique” case and stripped of his posts; the wrong was formally reviewed only years later. Chapter Six tells this story in full.

ch05.anchor: place him as a vice-chairman in Inner Mongolia or Ningxia
ch05.note: Vice-chairman is the deputy head of the government of an autonomous region (the counterpart of a provincial vice-governor); Chen Yangshan was finally posted to Ningxia in 1966, on the eve of the Cultural Revolution.

ch05.anchor: joined the Chinese Peasants' and Workers' Democratic Party
ch05.note: One of the small legal “democratic parties” of the People's Republic, descended from Deng Yanda's Third Party; membership marked a non-Communist figure aligned with the regime.

ch05.anchor: the noted jurist Minister Shi Liang
ch05.note: Shi Liang (1900-1985) was a celebrated woman lawyer, one of the “Seven Gentlemen” arrested in 1936 for their anti-Japanese stand, and the first Minister of Justice of the People's Republic.

ch05.anchor: Comrade Shangkun and Comrade Xiaoping
ch05.note: Yang Shangkun (1907-1998), then head of the Party Central Committee's General Office, and Deng Xiaoping. An Ziwen (1909-1980), named below, headed the Central Organization Department.

ch05.anchor: Bolshevik greetings
ch05.note: “Bolshevik greetings” (bu li) was a standard closing in Party correspondence of the period.

ch05.anchor: arranged for them to enjoy the middle-mess ration
ch05.note: Cadres and their dependents in the base areas were fed by grade — the “large,” “middle,” and “small” messes; Chen Yangshan refused the better ration for his children.

ch05.anchor: the chief responsible comrades of the Xi'an departments
ch05.note: The source prints 西安 (Xi'an) here where the sense plainly requires 公安 (public security), an evident misprint: the greater administrative regions and centrally administered municipalities had public security departments, and the conference was the national public security work conference. Rendered as printed, with the slip flagged.

ch05.anchor: his cousin came to Beijing to visit
ch05.note: The source refers to this relative as a paternal older cousin (tangxiong) twice and, in the next paragraph, once as a wife's older brother (qixiong); rendered consistently here as his cousin, the more frequent reading, which also agrees with the later mention of the man's wife as Chen Yangshan's cousin's wife.

ch05.anchor: the First Field Army had
ch05.note: One of the four great field armies into which the Communist forces were reorganized early in 1949. The First Field Army (Diyi Yezhanjun, 第一野战军), commanded by Peng Dehuai, cleared the northwest — Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia, Qinghai, and Xinjiang.

ch05.anchor: the Longhai Railway
ch05.note: The east–west trunk line (Longhai, 陇海) running from the Yellow Sea coast through Xi’an into Gansu; it was and remains the northwest’s main rail artery, which is why holding Xi’an commanded the whole region.

ch05.anchor: the Xi'an Military Control Commission was formed
ch05.note: The junguanhui (军事管制委员会), the temporary military-run administration installed in each city as the Communists took it, holding all authority until a civil government could be formed.

ch05.anchor: the newly established Ministry of Public Security
ch05.note: The People’s Republic’s police and internal-security ministry (Gong’an Bu, 公安部), set up in 1949 with Luo Ruiqing as its first minister; it ran the police, household registration, and the hunt for Kuomintang agents. First placed under the Central Military Commission, it soon passed to the State Council.

ch05.anchor: Li Shiying, Xu Jianguo, Wang Jinxiang, and Zhou Xing
ch05.note: Fellow security officials gathered for the conference. Li Shiying (1912–2001) became head of East China public security and later a deputy procurator-general; Xu Jianguo (1903–1977) became a deputy minister of public security and then an ambassador; Zhou Xing (1905–1975) became a deputy minister of public security and later first secretary of Yunnan. Wang Jinxiang was another security colleague.

ch05.anchor: the East China Military and Administrative Committee
ch05.note: One of the six ‘greater administrative regions’ (da xingzhengqu) into which China was divided from 1949 to 1954, each governed by a military-and-administrative committee standing between the central government and the provinces until the regular provincial structure took over.

ch05.anchor: the founding of the nation was proclaimed
ch05.note: The ceremony of October 1, 1949, at which Mao Zedong proclaimed the founding of the People’s Republic of China from the Tiananmen gate in Beijing, marking the Communist victory in the civil war.

ch05.anchor: among them Chen Yi, Pan Hannian
ch05.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), a marshal of the People’s Liberation Army, was the first mayor of Communist Shanghai and later foreign minister of the People’s Republic.

ch05.anchor: Wang Fan, and Yang Fan
ch05.note: Yang Fan (1912–1999), then a leading figure in the Shanghai public-security bureau. In 1955 he was arrested together with Pan Hannian on a fabricated charge and branded head of a ‘Pan-Yang counter-revolutionary clique’; he was held for some twenty-five years, and both men were cleared only after Mao’s death.

ch05.anchor: the Nanjing Municipal Procuratorate
ch05.note: The procuracy (jianchayuan, 检察院) is a Soviet-modeled organ separate from the courts, charged with prosecuting crimes and supervising the legality of state and judicial acts; its head is the chief procurator.

ch05.anchor: interrogating Huang Kai
ch05.note: The Kuomintang Central Statistics (Zhongtong) agent whose 1951 interrogation frames this chapter. By his own confession he took part through the early 1930s in breaking up Communist organizations in Wuhan, Shanghai, and Nanjing; he is little documented outside accounts of this case.

ch05.anchor: Luo Qiyuan and his wife
ch05.note: Luo Qiyuan (1894–1931), a Guangdong peasant-movement leader and an editor of the Party organ Red Flag; he was seized in Shanghai together with Yang Pao’an in the 1931 roundup and executed that August.

ch05.anchor: the Xinwen Bao, fabricating a declaration
ch05.note: The Xinwen Bao (新闻报) was, with the Shen Bao, one of Shanghai’s two largest commercial dailies. The forgers placed the fake notice across the city’s press; the other titles named below — the Shibao (时报) and Shishi Xinbao (时事新报) — were likewise major Shanghai papers of the day.

ch05.anchor: Zhou Enlai, and Lu Futan
ch05.note: Lu Futan (1890–1969), a former dockworker who rose to the Politburo Standing Committee. Arrested in Shanghai late in 1932, he defected and went over to the Kuomintang secret police; the Party had him secretly executed in 1969.

ch05.anchor: Tan Zhongyu, head of the Special Branch's action section
ch05.note: Tan Zhongyu directed the Special Branch’s action section (the armed ‘Red Squad’) in 1931. It was his men, keeping watch from a wonton stall, who confirmed Xiang Zhongfa’s defection, and he afterward sheltered Zhou Enlai in his own home.

ch05.anchor: Lu Futan, and Li Zhusheng
ch05.note: Li Zhusheng (1903–1973), a member of the provisional Central Politburo formed in Shanghai in 1931. Arrested in 1934, he too defected to the Kuomintang’s Central Statistics service.

ch05.anchor: lends the Chinese Eastern Railway for Japan to move troops
ch05.note: The Chinese Eastern Railway (中东铁路) was the Russian-built line across Manchuria, jointly held by China and the Soviet Union. The forged notice’s charges — that Moscow lent the line to Japan and had signed a nonaggression pact with Tokyo — were Kuomintang propaganda; no such Soviet-Japanese pact existed in 1932.

ch05.anchor: the All-China Federation of Trade Unions
ch05.note: The Communist Party’s national labor organization (中华全国总工会), founded in 1925 as the umbrella body of the country’s red trade unions.

ch05.anchor: Foreign lawyers enjoyed privileges in the concessions
ch05.note: Under the ‘unequal treaties,’ foreigners in China were exempt from Chinese law and answerable only to their own consular courts (extraterritoriality). A French lawyer in the foreign concession could therefore defy the Kuomintang with a freedom no Chinese lawyer possessed.

ch05.anchor: sending me to the Central Investigation Department
ch05.note: The Party’s central civilian intelligence organ (Zhongyang Diaocha Bu, 中央调查部), created in 1955 under Li Kenong to run foreign and domestic intelligence; it was a forerunner of today’s Ministry of State Security.

ch05.anchor: the First Order of August the First
ch05.note: The three highest military decorations, instituted in 1955 and awarded by era of service: the Order of August the First (八一勋章) for the founding of the Red Army, the Order of Independence and Freedom (独立自由勋章) for the war against Japan, and the Order of Liberation (解放勋章) for the civil war. ‘First’ denotes the first, or highest, class of each.

ch05.anchor: the great traitor Zhang Guotao
ch05.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979), a founding member of the Party and Mao Zedong’s chief rival in the mid-1930s. He broke with the leadership and defected to the Kuomintang in 1938; here Li Kenong is credited with intercepting him.

ch05.anchor: the later Chongqing negotiations
ch05.note: The talks of August to October 1945 at which Mao Zedong flew to Chiang Kai-shek’s wartime capital, Chongqing, to bargain over China’s postwar order; they yielded an agreement that soon broke down into civil war.

ch05.anchor: the War of Liberation may be called its high point
ch05.note: The Communist name for the civil war of 1946–1949 against the Kuomintang, which ended in the Communist conquest of the mainland and the founding of the People’s Republic.

ch05.anchor: Chen Yangshan always urged seeking truth from facts
ch05.note: Shishi qiushi (实事求是), ‘seek truth from facts’ — a classical phrase Mao Zedong adopted as a watchword for grounding policy in real conditions rather than dogma or pressure from above; Chen invokes it here against inflated case quotas.

ch05.anchor: Zhou Enlai and Song Qingling too
ch05.note: Song Qingling (1893–1981), the widow of Sun Yat-sen and a sister-in-law of Chiang Kai-shek, who sided with the Communists and became an honorary head of state of the People’s Republic.

ch05.anchor: Hu Di, Song Zaisheng, and others
ch05.note: Song Zaisheng, a Special Branch intelligence man who, like the ‘three heroes of Longtan,’ was planted inside the enemy apparatus — he served as a political investigator in the Nationalist Shanghai-Wusong Garrison Command.

ch05.anchor: run into Chen Long
ch05.note: Chen Long (1910–1958), a veteran security officer who had guarded Mao Zedong at the 1945 Chongqing talks; after 1949 he was public-security chief of Nanjing and rose to deputy minister of public security.

ch05.anchor: startling the snake by beating the grass
ch05.note: A Chinese set phrase, dacao jingshe (打草惊蛇), ‘beat the grass and startle the snake’ — to alarm and scatter an adversary by a premature or clumsy move that gives one’s hand away.

ch06.anchor: the Five-Antis
ch06.note: The Five-Antis campaign of 1952 struck at private business owners for bribery, tax evasion, theft of state property, cheating on contracts, and stealing state economic secrets; it ran alongside the Three-Antis, aimed at officials (see the note there). Printed folio 194.

ch06.anchor: an Anti-Rightist Campaign
ch06.note: Launched in mid-1957 after the brief liberalization of the Hundred Flowers, the Anti-Rightist Campaign turned on those who had criticized the Party at its invitation. Well over half a million people were labeled Rightists; the Party itself later called the campaign gravely over-extended and reversed most of the verdicts, as the book goes on to describe. Printed folio 195.

ch06.anchor: the Fourth National Conference on Political and Legal Work
ch06.note: Held in June 1958, at the height of the leftward turn. It was here that the friction between the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Public Security was worked up into the 'anti-Party clique' case that would cost Chen Yangshan and his colleagues twenty years. Printed folio 195.

ch06.anchor: the Ministry of Justice was abolished
ch06.note: The ministry was not merely reorganized but shut down: its functions passed to the Supreme People's Court, and it was not re-established until 1979. The 'anti-Party clique' verdict was thus bound up with the abolition of the institution itself. Printed folio 196.

ch06.anchor: Dong Biwu, then president of the Supreme People's Court
ch06.note: Dong Biwu (1886-1975) was one of the handful who founded the Chinese Communist Party in 1921, and President of the Supreme People's Court from 1954 to 1959; he later served as acting head of state. That so senior a figure dissented from the 'anti-Party clique' finding, as the text records, is corroborated by later Party accounts of the case. Printed folio 196.

ch06.anchor: "On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People"
ch06.note: Mao Zedong's speech of February 1957, published in revised form that June, drew a line between 'contradictions among the people,' to be handled by persuasion, and 'contradictions between the enemy and ourselves.' The Ministry of Justice group was condemned for applying that very distinction to criminal justice. Printed folio 196.

ch06.anchor: deputy manager of the Qinghe Woolen Mill
ch06.note: A steep fall for a vice-minister: the mill lay at Qinghe, then a town in Changping County north of Beijing. Printed folio 196.

ch06.anchor: the Draft History of the Central Special Branch, more than a hundred thousand words
ch06.note: Chen Yangshan's manuscript, written over three years after Li Kenong's death, became a foundational internal source on the Party's first intelligence organ. It grew out of the materials-gathering project Li Kenong had proposed in 1961 (see his letter appended to Chapter 5). Printed folio 197.

ch06.anchor: the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference
ch06.note: The enlarged Central Work Conference of January-February 1962 drew some seven thousand cadres to Beijing to take stock of the disastrous Great Leap Forward and the famine that followed. It is remembered as a moment of relative candor and self-criticism within the leadership. Printed folio 199.

ch06.anchor: a branch campus of the College of Foreign Affairs
ch06.note: The College of Foreign Affairs, founded in Beijing in 1955 under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, trained diplomats. Printed folio 199.

ch06.anchor: a vice-chairman of the government of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region
ch06.note: Ningxia, established as an autonomous region for the Hui (Chinese Muslims) in 1958, lies in the arid northwest with its capital at Yinchuan. For an ailing man of sixty from the Yangtze delta it was a hard and distant posting, as the text stresses. Printed folio 199.

ch06.anchor: the Shanghai rebels' seizure of power
ch06.note: The 'January Storm' of 1967, in which rebel groups in Shanghai seized power from the city's Party and government, set off a wave of such seizures across the country and deepened the chaos of the Cultural Revolution. Printed folio 200.

ch06.anchor: a preparatory group for the revolutionary committee
ch06.note: Revolutionary committees were the new organs of power of the Cultural Revolution, combining army officers, veteran cadres, and mass representatives in a 'three-in-one' body that took over from the dismantled Party and government structures. Printed folio 200.

ch06.anchor: the Nationalists' Nanjing Reflection Institute
ch06.note: The Nationalist government ran 'reflection institutes' (fanxingyuan) where captured Communists were held and pressed to recant. The Nanjing one was among the most notorious. Printed folio 200.

ch06.anchor: went over again, to Wang Jingwei
ch06.note: Wang Jingwei (1883-1944), once a leading figure of the Nationalists, defected during the war with Japan and in 1940 headed the Japanese-sponsored puppet government at Nanjing; his name became a byword for collaboration. Printed folio 201.

ch06.anchor: Huo Shilian succeeded him as first secretary
ch06.note: Huo Shilian (1909-1996) led the Ningxia Party organization in the 1970s and later Shanxi. Printed folio 201.

ch06.anchor: The Sixth Plenary Session of the Tenth Central Committee, held in June 1981
ch06.note: The source misdates the plenum. The Resolution named here was in fact adopted at the Sixth Plenary Session of the ELEVENTH Central Committee, in June 1981; there was no such plenum of the Tenth. The rendering keeps the printed text; a few lines later the book gives the correct Third Plenary Session of the Eleventh Central Committee, which makes the slip plain. Printed folio 202.

ch06.anchor: the Third Plenary Session of the Eleventh Central Committee
ch06.note: The plenum of December 1978 that turned the Party toward reform and opening and set in motion the wholesale reversal of the political cases of the Mao years, Chen Yangshan's among them. Printed folio 202.

ch06.anchor: a deputy procurator-general of the Supreme People's Procuratorate
ch06.note: The Supreme People's Procuratorate, the state's prosecuting organ, had been abolished during the Cultural Revolution and was restored under the 1978 constitution; Chen Yangshan helped rebuild it. Printed folio 202.

ch06.anchor: first to bear the world's cares and last to enjoy its pleasures
ch06.note: The famous close of Fan Zhongyan's 'Record of the Yueyang Tower' (1046): to be first in the realm to worry over its troubles and last to enjoy its pleasures. The line became the classic Chinese ideal of the public-minded official. Printed folio 209.

ch06.anchor: the martyr Rou Shi
ch06.note: Rou Shi (1902-1931), pen name of Zhao Pingfu, a native of Ninghai, was a writer close to Lu Xun and one of the 'Five Martyrs of the Left League' shot at Longhua. Lu Xun's essay 'In Memory of the Forgotten' mourns him. Printed folio 206.

ch06.anchor: twenty-four comrades in all
ch06.note: On January 17, 1931, twenty-some Communists, Rou Shi, Lin Yunan, He Mengxiong, and Li Qiushi among them, were arrested at a Shanghai hotel and shot at Longhua on February 7 (see the note on Longhua in Chapter 1). Chen Yangshan's charge that the Wang Ming leadership deliberately let them be taken reflects the bitter factional reading of the survivors; historians link the arrests to the internal fight over Wang Ming's line but do not all accept that the betrayal was deliberate. Printed folio 206.

ch06.anchor: the People's Daily published an article
ch06.note: The People's Daily is the official organ of the Party's Central Committee; a formal obituary in its pages fixed Chen Yangshan's standing in the Party's own record. Printed folio 209.

ch06.anchor: Xiao Taihuang
ch06.note: The same murdered Special Branch comrade is named Xiao Shouhuang (肖寿煌) in Chapter 3 and in Appendix II; here, and only here, the source writes his given name as 肖太煌 (Xiao Taihuang). Both are the book's own forms for one man; each is left as printed rather than silently harmonized.

ch06.anchor: a broad and searching Rectification Movement
ch06.note: The 1957 Rectification Movement (zhengfeng, 整风), a Party-wide drive opened that April inviting outsiders to criticize cadres’ bureaucratism and privilege — the open-criticism phase soon known as the Hundred Flowers. When the criticism cut deeper than the leadership expected, it was abruptly reversed into the Anti-Rightist Campaign that swept up Chen and his colleagues. It is distinct from the wartime Yan’an Rectification of 1942–45.

ch06.anchor: The State Council's Political and Legal Affairs Office
ch06.note: The government (State Council) office that coordinated the courts, the procuratorates, and the public-security and justice ministries — the administrative counterpart to the Party’s own Central Political-Legal Group, which set policy in this field.

ch06.anchor: Zheng Shaowen, secretary of the ministry's
ch06.note: Zheng Shaowen (郑绍文, 1905–1993), a Sichuanese who joined the Party in 1927 and was jailed four times as a Shanghai underground organizer; vice-minister of justice from 1954 and secretary of the ministry’s Party group. After this case was finally reversed he became a vice-president of the Supreme People’s Court in 1979.

ch06.anchor: Wang Huai'an, Party group member
ch06.note: Wang Huai’an (王怀安, 1915–2015), a Sichuan law graduate and judge, member of the ministry’s Party group; alone of the nine he was branded a Rightist and expelled from the Party. Persecuted again in the Cultural Revolution, he served from 1979 as a criminal-division chief and vice-president of the Supreme People’s Court.

ch06.anchor: speaking out freely and airing views in the open
ch06.note: ‘Speaking out freely and airing views’ (da ming da fang, 大鸣大放) and ‘great democracy’ (da minzhu, 大民主) were the mass-mobilization methods of the period: open denunciation meetings and big-character posters at which any remark could be, as the text says, ‘raised to the level of principle’ and turned against the speaker.

ch06.anchor: sent to the Central Political-Legal Group
ch06.note: The Central Political-Legal Group (中央政法小组), set up by the Party in June 1958 under Peng Zhen to direct the courts, procuratorates, and the security and justice ministries. It was this body that pressed the ‘anti-Party clique’ label on the Ministry of Justice over Dong Biwu’s objection, and it insisted on upholding the verdict at each later review.

ch06.anchor: the Organic Law of the People's Courts
ch06.note: The Organic Law of the People’s Courts, enacted by the National People’s Congress in 1954, established the court system and, following the 1954 constitution, declared that courts tried cases independently and were subject only to the law. That principle of independent trial was among the first casualties of the leftward turn recounted here and was dropped altogether in the 1975 constitution.

ch06.anchor: placed on one year's probation within the Party
ch06.note: ‘Probation within the Party’ (liu dang chakan, 留党察看) is the severest Party penalty short of expulsion: the member keeps his card but loses his rights for a fixed term, pending a final ruling on whether he is cast out. To be ‘demoted three grades’ was a parallel cut in the administrative cadre rank that fixed a man’s salary, housing, and standing.

ch06.anchor: His youngest son, Chen Zhenyu
ch06.note: Chen Yangshan’s youngest son. The account here — that the shock of his father’s sudden disgrace brought on a mental illness from which he never recovered — is one of the book’s few glimpses of the toll the campaigns took on the families of the accused, not only on the accused themselves.

ch06.anchor: seeking truth from facts
ch06.note: ‘Seeking truth from facts’ (shishi qiu shi, 实事求是), a phrase from the History of the Han that Mao made a watchword of Party method and that Deng Xiaoping revived after 1978 as the banner of the reform era, against dogmatism and the excesses of the campaigns.

ch06.anchor: following the mass line
ch06.note: The ‘mass line’ (qunzhong luxian, 群众路线), the Party’s doctrine that leaders should gather the scattered views of the people, refine them into policy, and carry them back to the people — invoked here as one of the ‘fine ways’ the leftward years had trampled.

ch06.anchor: the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection
ch06.note: In 1962 the Party’s standing disciplinary organ was in fact the Central Control Commission (中央监察委员会), chaired since 1955 by Dong Biwu; the body properly called the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection had lapsed in 1955 and was not re-established until 1978. It found that the nine had made work errors but had committed no acts against the Party — a finding the Central Political-Legal Group refused to accept.

ch06.anchor: after the Spring Festival went off
ch06.note: The Spring Festival (Chunjie, 春节) is the Chinese lunar New Year, the year’s chief family holiday; Chen set out for his distant post, alone, only once the festival was past.

ch06.anchor: reached Yinchuan
ch06.note: Yinchuan, capital of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region: an old garrison and trading city on the Yellow River in the arid northwest, more than a thousand kilometres from Beijing, whose harsh climate the ailing Chen had rightly feared.

ch06.anchor: The rebels were forever coming
ch06.note: ‘Rebels’ (zaofanpai, 造反派) were the militant mass factions of the Cultural Revolution, licensed by Mao’s call to rebel against those in authority. They stormed offices, seized power from Party and government organs, and hauled officials before ‘struggle sessions’ of public accusation and abuse, as befell Chen below.

ch06.anchor: carried off those they called
ch06.note: ‘Royalists’ (baohuangpai, 保皇派, literally ‘protect-the-emperor faction’) was the rebels’ jeer for rival mass groups and for cadres who defended the standing Party leadership instead of overthrowing it.

ch06.anchor: with Kang Jianmin as its head
ch06.note: Kang Jianmin (康健民, 1916–1977), a Gansu-born cavalry officer of the Red Army made a major-general in 1955; chairman of the Ningxia revolutionary committee from 1968 and first secretary of the region’s Party committee from 1971 until his death in January 1977, when Huo Shilian succeeded him.

ch06.anchor: the Gang of Four had been smashed
ch06.note: The ‘Gang of Four’ — Mao’s widow Jiang Qing and her Shanghai allies Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen — were the radical leaders blamed for the worst of the Cultural Revolution. Their arrest on October 6, 1976, weeks after Mao’s death, ended the Cultural Revolution and opened the way to the reversals of verdicts, Chen’s among them, described here.

ch06.anchor: grasping revolution to promote production
ch06.note: ‘Grasp revolution, promote production’ (zhua geming, cu shengchan, 抓革命促生产), a standing slogan of the era asserting that political struggle need not be allowed to harm the economy — here, that the campaign against the fallen radicals should go hand in hand with rebuilding output.

ch06.anchor: a deputy to the National People's Congress
ch06.note: The National People’s Congress, the highest organ of state and China’s national legislature, which meets in Beijing; its several thousand deputies are chosen indirectly, and election as one was a mark of standing — here, of political rehabilitation.

ch06.anchor: in the History of Our Party Since the Founding of the People's Republic
ch06.note: The second of the Party’s two great ‘historical resolutions,’ adopted in 1981, which assessed the whole Mao era, condemned the Cultural Revolution, and weighed Mao’s merits against his errors. It is distinct from the 1945 resolution of nearly the same name (which covered the Party’s pre-1949 history); as the note on the plenum records, the source misdates the session that adopted it.

ch06.anchor: made by the Eighth National Congress
ch06.note: The Eighth National Congress of the Party (September 1956) declared that socialist transformation was in the main complete and that the task ahead was economic construction under a strengthened ‘socialist legality.’ Its moderate line was soon overtaken by the leftward turn — which is why loyalty to it counted for the ministry’s defence at this final review.

ch06.anchor: at the request of Liu Fuzhi
ch06.note: Liu Fuzhi (刘复之, 1917–2013), a Guangdong-born veteran who joined the Party in 1938; procurator-general of the Supreme People’s Procuratorate from 1988 to 1993, and at other times minister of public security and minister of justice.

ch00.note: Zhang Baijia (章百家, b. 1948), a historian of the Chinese Communist Party, its foreign relations, and the reform era. He was deputy director of the Party's Central Party History Research Office from 2004 to 2011, and by the byline held the post of deputy chairman of the society named there. This is a general preface to the whole book series, not to Chen Yangshan's life in particular. (His career here is corroborated by his official academic biography.)

The publisher's series to which this book belongs (隐蔽战线春秋书系), issued by the CCP Party History Press. The hidden front (隐蔽战线) is the standard Chinese term for the Party's clandestine intelligence, security, and counter-espionage work, set against the open military and political struggle. The series runs in three strands — a biography set, a memoir set, and a set of historical accounts; this volume belongs to the biography set.

Xu Xiangqian (徐向前, 1901–1990), one of the ten marshals of the People's Liberation Army and later minister of national defense. His complaint that the Party's official histories slighted intelligence work is a real and recurring one: that work could not be written up while its methods and its agents still had to be protected.

The Chinese Communist name for the 1919–1949 phase of the revolution, from the May Fourth movement to the founding of the People's Republic — led, in the theory, by the proletariat but still bourgeois-democratic in its immediate aims, as opposed to the socialist revolution held to begin after 1949. The framing is Mao Zedong's.

ch00.anchor: At the height of the White Terror
ch00.note: The "White Terror" (白色恐怖) is the standard name for the waves of arrest and killing the Kuomintang loosed on Communists and their sympathizers after Chiang Kai-shek's break with the Party in April 1927. "White," the color of counter-revolution, stands against the Communists' red.

ch00.anchor: the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army
ch00.note: The Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army (中国工农红军), the Communist army built from 1927–28 out of the failed uprisings and led by commanders such as Zhu De and Mao Zedong. It fought the Kuomintang through the base-area years and the Long March; in 1937, under the anti-Japanese united front, its main forces were redesignated the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army.

The weijiao (围剿), or "encirclement and suppression," campaigns were the successive Kuomintang offensives of 1930–1934 that sought to destroy the Communist soviet base areas, above all the Central Soviet in Jiangxi. The fifth campaign broke the Jiangxi base and forced the Long March.

ch00.anchor: the anti-Japanese national united front into being
ch00.note: The Second United Front (1937–1945), the wartime alliance of the Communists and the Kuomintang against Japan, following the first alliance of 1924–1927 (Chapter 1). Forged after the Xi'an Incident, it left the two parties nominally cooperating while each kept its own army and territory, and it frayed steadily as the war wore on.

ch00.anchor: During the War of Resistance the Center
ch00.note: The War of Resistance Against Japan (抗日战争), China's war with Japan of 1937–1945 — the Chinese theater of what the West calls the Second Sino-Japanese War, and part of the wider Second World War.

ch00.anchor: In the War of Liberation the intelligence and security work
ch00.note: The War of Liberation (解放战争), the Communist name for the final phase of the Chinese civil war, 1946–1949, which ended in the Communist victory, the founding of the People's Republic, and the Nationalist retreat to Taiwan.

ch07.note: This first appendix is Chen Yangshan's official obituary, cast in the fixed form of a Chinese Communist Party memorial notice (悼词): a formal recital of ranks and services in the celebratory language of the genre. Its facts can be checked against the narrative chapters; its verdicts are the Party's own.

The obituary and the chronology (Appendix III) both date the full clearing of Chen Yangshan's name to the aftermath of the December 1978 Third Plenum, which reversed the verdicts of the Mao era wholesale. Chapter 6, following the case papers, is more exact: the 1978–79 review quashed the "anti-Party clique" verdict but let stand a residual finding of "grave Right deviation," and only the reexamination of 1983 negated that too and reversed the case thoroughly. The discrepancy is between the general political turn of 1978 and the particular act that closed his case five years later.

ch07.anchor: one central task and two basic points
ch07.note: A slogan of the reform era (一个中心、两个基本点): the "one central task" is economic construction; the "two basic points" are upholding the Four Cardinal Principles and pursuing reform and opening. It was codified as the Party's "basic line" at the Thirteenth Congress in 1987.

Deng Xiaoping's four non-negotiable commitments, laid down in 1979 as the bounds of the reform-era opening: to the socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought.

The state economic plans in force when the obituary was written: the Ten-Year Program (1991–2000) and the Eighth Five-Year Plan (1991–1995), adopted at the Seventh Plenum of the Thirteenth Central Committee late in 1990. Tying the dead man's example to the Party's current tasks is a convention of the form.

Jiang Zemin (1926–2022) became general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party in June 1989, in the aftermath of the Tiananmen crackdown, and led it until 2002. "With Comrade Jiang Zemin at its core" was the set phrase of the day for the Party leadership.

ch07.anchor: the Party's Fa'nan district committee in Shanghai
ch07.note: The Fa’nan (法南) district committee took in the southern part of the Shanghai French Concession (法租界), one of the Party’s territorial sub-organizations in the city. As its propaganda chief and a distribution officer, the young Chen handled the clandestine printing and circulation of Party literature.

The ‘people’s democratic dictatorship’ (人民民主专政), the formula Mao Zedong set out in 1949 for the new state: rule exercised by a coalition of classes led by the working class over its class enemies. It remains the official constitutional self-description of the People’s Republic.

‘Bourgeois liberalization’ (资产阶级自由化) was the reform era’s label for calls for Western-style political freedoms and multiparty democracy; campaigns against it ran through the 1980s. The charge carried particular weight in this obituary, composed less than two years after the suppression of the 1989 protests.

ch07.anchor: the Party's Seventh Plenary Session of the Thirteenth Central Committee
ch07.note: Held in Beijing on December 25–30, 1990, this plenum adopted the Party’s proposal for the Ten-Year Program and the Eighth Five-Year Plan (both named in the next lines) and heard a keynote address by Jiang Zemin. Invoking ‘its spirit’ dates the obituary firmly to 1991.

ch08.note: This appendix gathers Chen Yangshan's own writing, found among his papers after his death. The four pieces are his, in the first person: (1) retells, in a plainer and earlier version, the Bao Junfu affair of Chapter 2; (2), with its appended profiles, returns to the four Central Special Branch comrades whom Kang Sheng framed, the subject of Chapter 3; (3) is the bare outline of the memoir he did not live to write; and (4) his household rules for his children. Where they touch the narrative chapters, the two can be read against each other.

The January 28 Incident was the Japanese attack on Shanghai that began on January 28, 1932. Chen's memoir here dates Bao Junfu's release to 1933, the year after; the affair and the release are not the same date.

Cheng Jianyu (程建宇), Chen Yangshan's eldest son, who assembled these papers. He signs with the surname Cheng (程), the family's original name: his father had changed his own surname from Cheng to Chen on entering underground work (see Chapter 1), and the son kept the older form.

The recognition was thus left half-made: Wu Hujing was named a revolutionary martyr in 1957, but without the certificate that would have secured his family's standing and support. It is exactly the kind of unfinished rehabilitation the letter above was written to press.
Cao Yi'ou was Kang Sheng's wife; Su Mei, wife of the murdered Xiao Shouhuang, was her younger sister. The four dead men had stood close to Kang Sheng himself, and the nearness did not spare them.

ch08.anchor: A Letter to the Central Organization Department and the Ministry of State Security
ch08.note: This is the 1988 letter reproduced as a document, from the manuscript shown above in facsimile, together with the four attached biographies. The same letter is quoted within the narrative of Chapter 3; the two renderings follow the source's own two printings of it.

Shanghai University (上海大学), founded in 1922 as a joint Nationalist–Communist venture and in practice led by the Communists, was a gathering place for the revolutionary young: Yu Youren was its nominal president and Qu Qiubai directed its sociology department. The Nationalists shut it down after the April 12, 1927 coup. To have lived beside it and known many there marks Bao Junfu’s early left-wing ties.

ch08.anchor: the peasant uprising I had organized in Zhejiang
ch08.note: Corroborated by the standard accounts: after seeing He Long safely away toward Honghu in 1927, Chen returned to his native Shangyu in Zhejiang and tried to raise a peasant revolt. Its failure early in 1928 drove him back to Shanghai and into the lodging at Bao Junfu’s house described here.

The Communist Party’s Central Organization Department (中央组织部) — a different body from the Kuomintang department of the same name in section (1) above — controls Party personnel and cadre appointments and is among the most powerful organs of the Chinese system; Zhou Enlai headed it in the late 1920s. Chen asks it to direct local Party-history offices to investigate the four murdered comrades, since without such a notice the local offices would not act.

ch08.anchor: the White areas under Wang Ming's
ch08.note: ‘White areas’ (白区) was the Communist term for territory under Nationalist control, as opposed to the Party’s own ‘Red’ base areas. Underground work in the White areas — the clandestine struggle in enemy-held cities — is what much of this memoir outline recounts.

ch09.anchor: A Chronology of Chen Yangshan's Life
ch09.note: A 年谱, the year-by-year chronicle of a life that is a standing genre of Chinese biography. It agrees in the main with the narrative chapters and the obituary; where it dates the undoing of his 1958 case — part of the penalty lifted in 1962, the verdict reversed in 1978 — it can be read against Chapter 6, which follows the case papers and places the thorough clearing of his name in 1983.

The pseudonyms Chen Yangshan worked under in the underground. He had already changed his surname from Cheng to Chen (see Chapter 1); a professional of the hidden front took a fresh name for each posting, and "Lao Wang" — "Old Wang" — is a plain alias of the kind used among comrades. Several of these names recur in the narrative chapters.

ch09.anchor: the Hankou Young Men's Self-Improvement Society
ch09.note: A small patriotic self-study group Chen organized among young workers in Hankou in the wake of the February 7 strike, to "seek the truth of how to save the country." It is little documented outside accounts of his own life.

ch09.anchor: entrusted by Wang Yifei, secretary-general of the Central Military Commission
ch09.note: Wang Yifei (Wang Yifei, 王一飞, 1898–1928), like Chen a native of Shangyu, was among the Party's earliest trained military men — he studied at the Frunze Academy in Moscow — and became the first secretary-general of the CCP Central Military Commission, working under Zhou Enlai. Sent late in 1927 to reorganize the Hunan provincial committee, he was betrayed and shot at Changsha in January 1928.

ch09.anchor: a peasant uprising in Haimen county, Zhejiang
ch09.note: Haimen, a coastal town of Taizhou in eastern Zhejiang (today the Jiaojiang district of Taizhou). Communist-led risings and a garrison mutiny there in 1928 are recorded in local Party history, though this particular episode is known chiefly from Chen's own account.

ch09.anchor: the New Sichuan News Agency in Chongqing
ch09.note: One of the open news agencies the Party's intelligence apparatus ran as a front, on the model of the earlier South China News Agency in Shanghai (Chapter 2). Under its cover Chen and his colleagues gathered intelligence and carried on united-front work in the Sichuan cities.

ch09.anchor: the Fifth Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference
ch09.note: The Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, founded in 1949, is the united-front advisory body that draws the small legal "democratic parties" and non-Party notables into the political system. A place on its national committee marks a person's standing rather than any Party office; the "Fifth" here is its fifth national committee, seated in 1978.

ch10.note: The author's source list, rendered here with each title in romanization, an English gloss in brackets, and the publisher and year as printed; no bibliographic detail has been added. Several entries bear on how the book was sourced: two — the life of Wu Kejian and the newspaper serial "The Secret War of the Special Branch" — are by Yao Huafei, this book's own author; and the memorial volume Essays in Memory of Chen Yangshan, together with the closing line of memoirs and papers by Chen and his family and comrades, are materials close to the subject. It is a fair picture of a Party biography built in good part from the recollections of the man's own circle.

ch10.anchor: Mao Zedong]. Central Party Literature Press
ch10.note: The Central Party Literature Press (中央文献出版社) is the Communist Party's own imprint for the authorized lives of its leaders. Several works cited here are of its standard official kinds: a zhuan (传) is a full biography and a nianpu (年谱) a year-by-year chronicle of a life, both compiled from Party archives and treated as authoritative.

A few of the sources are Nationalist-side accounts published in Taiwan, this one a history of the Kuomintang's military-intelligence bureau (Juntong). Their presence shows the author drew on the other side's literature as well as the mainland's, even where the two remain far apart on the events.

ch11.note: Chen Yangshan was born on October 7, 1906 (the chronology in Appendix III gives the same date), so this was the centenary of his birth. To mark it, the China Friendship Publishing Company brought out a first version of the book that September under the title The Legend of Chen Yangshan, Lucky General of the Hidden Front. The present volume is the expanded rewrite the author describes here, reworked over the following decade. Fujiang (福将, 'lucky general') is a stock phrase for a commander who comes through every danger unharmed.
Diehai Liaowang (谊海痼望), literally 'a lookout over the sea of espionage': a Chinese periodical on the history and craft of intelligence work. The English here renders the title's sense.

ch11.anchor: to be borne by your bureau's Comrade Yao Huafei
ch11.note: Yao Huafei (姚华飞, b. 1947), a Shaanxi-born writer and member of the China Writers' Association who specialized in the history of the Communist intelligence services. Commissioned by the state-security authorities, he wrote several such works, among them accounts of the martyred radio operator Li Bai and of the agent Shen Anna as well as this life of Chen Yangshan; each was vetted by the state-security departments before it appeared.

ch11.anchor: The Legend of Chen Yangshan, Lucky General of the Hidden Front
ch11.note: The book's own first version, published by the China Friendship Publishing Company in September 2006 for the centenary of Chen's birth. The author explains here that he went on gathering material for more than a decade afterward and rewrote the manuscript six times to make the present, fuller biography.

ch11.anchor: Ling Yun, Liu Fuzhi, and other comrades wrote inscriptions
ch11.note: Ling Yun (凌云, 1917–2018) was a veteran of the Party's wartime Central Department of Social Affairs who rose to deputy minister of public security and, in 1983, became the first minister of the newly created Ministry of State Security. An inscription from him, and from the former procurator-general Liu Fuzhi, lent the book weighty official endorsement.
